The largest known beaver dam, in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, is around 850 metres long and was spotted on satellite images.

fun_zoo_lovers_day.intro: For everyone who still gets excited at the penguin enclosure. A day to visit a zoo, watch keepers at work and remember childhood afternoons among the animals.
funFacts: Tiergarten Schönbrunn in Vienna opened in 1752 and is the oldest zoo still operating anywhere in the world.
The short word zoo comes from London's Zoological Gardens, which opened to the general public in 1847.
Przewalski's horse survived only in zoos for decades before breeding programmes returned it to the Mongolian steppe.

fun_unicorn_day.intro: Glitter, rainbows and one impossible horn. Unicorn Day celebrates a creature that never existed and yet turns up on cakes, socks and carousels everywhere.
funFacts: The unicorn is Scotland's national animal and appears in the royal coat of arms.
Medieval traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, fetching many times their weight in gold.
The Greek physician Ctesias described a one-horned animal in India around 400 BC, one of the oldest written accounts.

fun_siblings_day.intro: Brothers and sisters get their own date: a day to send an old photo, apologise for something from 1998 and admit that nobody else shares quite the same memories.
funFacts: Claudia Evart founded the day in the US in memory of her siblings and chose the birthday of her sister for the date.
The bond usually lasts longer than any other in life, beginning before friendships and outliving the parents.
Identical twins share almost identical genes but still have completely different fingerprints.

fun_pet_day.intro: A day for the animals that share our sofas. Dogs, cats, rabbits, hamsters and everything in between get an extra walk, an extra treat and far too many photos.
funFacts: Dogs were the first domesticated animals; finds in Germany show people and dogs buried together over 14,000 years ago.
A cat's nose print is as individual as a human fingerprint, right down to the pattern of ridges.
Goldfish remember training cues for months, which makes the famous three-second memory a myth.

fun_yuris_night.intro: Also known as the World Space Party: on 12 April, space fans throw parties, screenings and observatory nights to mark the first human flight into orbit.
funFacts: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin circled the Earth once in 108 minutes aboard Vostok 1.
Exactly twenty years later, on 12 April 1981, the first Space Shuttle lifted off on its maiden flight.
For the 50th anniversary in 2011 the party ran at more than 567 events in 75 countries on all seven continents.

fun_scrabble_day.intro: The day of the letter tile, held on the birthday of the man who invented the game. Perfect for arguing about whether a word really exists.
funFacts: Architect Alfred Mosher Butts invented the game in the 1930s and first called it Lexiko, then Criss Cross Words.
He worked out the letter frequencies by counting characters on the front page of the New York Times.
The standard English edition contains four S tiles; letter distributions differ between language editions.

fun_dolphin_day.intro: Clever, curious and permanently grinning: a day for dolphins, the marine mammals that surf bow waves and seem to enjoy an audience.
funFacts: Dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time so they keep surfacing to breathe.
Every bottlenose dolphin develops a signature whistle that works like a name and gets answered by others.
The orca is the largest member of the dolphin family, which belongs to the toothed whales.

fun_world_art_day.intro: Held on Leonardo da Vinci's birthday, World Art Day invites everyone into museums, studios and open workshops, and encourages people to simply pick up a brush.
funFacts: The date is Leonardo da Vinci's birthday: he was born on 15 April 1452 near Vinci in Tuscany.
The International Association of Art launched the day in 2012, and UNESCO adopted it as a world day in 2019.
The Mona Lisa has no eyebrows, one of the small oddities visitors queue in the Louvre to check for themselves.

fun_eggs_benedict_day.intro: Toasted muffin, ham, a poached egg and a spoonful of hollandaise: the most luxurious way to eat breakfast, and a dish that brunch menus refuse to give up.
funFacts: Two New York stories compete for the invention: Delmonico's restaurant and a hangover order at the Waldorf in 1894.
Hollandaise is an emulsion of egg yolk and butter; if it splits, a splash of cold water often brings it back.
Poaching works without the shell in barely simmering water, and a dash of vinegar helps the white set quickly.

fun_bat_appreciation_day.intro: Spring is when bats leave their winter roosts, so mid-April is a fitting moment to appreciate the only mammals that truly fly and the insects they clear from our evenings.
funFacts: Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight; everything else that glides is merely falling with style.
There are more than 1,400 bat species, which makes roughly one in five mammal species a bat.
The bumblebee bat weighs about two grams and is considered the smallest mammal in the world.

fun_pinata_day.intro: Blindfold, stick, three turns and swing: the piñata turns any party into a small competition. A day for papier-mâché animals filled with sweets.
funFacts: The classic star piñata has seven points, which originally stood for the seven deadly sins.
The oldest versions were clay pots; today most piñatas are papier-mâché built over a balloon.
Similar smashing customs existed in Europe and in China long before the piñata became a Mexican fixture.

fun_garlic_day.intro: A day for the bulb that quietly improves almost every savoury dish on earth, and that people have been growing, plaiting and hanging up for thousands of years.
funFacts: Garlic only smells once it is damaged: cutting or crushing turns a precursor compound into pungent allicin.
According to Herodotus, the workers who built the pyramids were rationed garlic and onions.
Gilroy in California calls itself the garlic capital and its festival famously served garlic ice cream.

fun_pineapple_upside_down_cake_day.intro: Baked bottom up in a skillet and flipped onto the plate, so caramelised pineapple rings and glacé cherries end up on top. A retro cake that never really left.
funFacts: The cake bakes with the fruit underneath, and only the flip at the end puts the caramelised rings on show.
It became a household name after a 1925 recipe contest for canned pineapple that drew around 60,000 entries.
Pineapples do not grow on trees: each low bromeliad plant produces just one fruit at a time.

fun_bulldogs_are_beautiful_day.intro: Wrinkled face, broad chest, unhurried walk: the bulldog will never win a beauty contest — which is exactly the point today. A day for the most charming squashed nose around.
funFacts: The breed goes back to dogs bred for bull-baiting; Britain banned the spectacle in 1835.
Over 80 per cent of bulldog litters are delivered by caesarean, because the heads are so large.
Yale University has had a bulldog mascot called Handsome Dan since 1889.

fun_jelly_bean_day.intro: Small, shiny and impossible to eat just one of: jelly beans get their own day, ideally poured into a jar so the colours can be sorted before eating.
funFacts: The glossy shell comes from panning, a slow coating technique also used for sugared almonds.
Ronald Reagan loved them so much that a blue variety was created for his 1981 inauguration.
Making them takes days: the chewy centre is moulded and dried before layer after layer of syrup and sugar goes on.

fun_german_beer_day.intro: Germany raises a glass to its brewing tradition on the anniversary of the 1516 purity law, from wheat beer in the south to pilsner in the north.
funFacts: On 23 April 1516 the Bavarian dukes decreed in Ingolstadt that beer should contain only barley, hops and water.
Yeast was missing from that list simply because nobody knew it existed yet.
German brewers have marked the day since 1995, and around 1,500 breweries are still at work in the country.

fun_pigs_in_a_blanket_day.intro: Little sausages wrapped in dough, served warm from the tray. The party snack that disappears fastest gets a day of its own.
funFacts: In the US they are cocktail sausages in pastry; in Britain the name means sausages wrapped in bacon at Christmas.
The first printed recipe under this name appeared in a Betty Crocker cookbook for children in 1957.
German kitchens make a close relative called Würstchen im Schlafrock, sausages in a dressing gown of dough.

fun_world_penguin_day.intro: Tuxedos, waddling and belly slides: late April is when Adélie penguins head north, and the date has become a worldwide celebration of penguins in general.
funFacts: There are around 18 penguin species, all in the southern hemisphere, though the Galápagos penguin reaches the equator.
Emperor penguins dive more than 500 metres deep and can stay under water for over 20 minutes.
The date is tied to the annual northward migration of Adélie penguins away from their Antarctic colonies.

fun_pretzel_day.intro: Knotted, glossy and sprinkled with coarse salt: the pretzel gets its own day. Whether Bavarian Breze or soft American street pretzel, the shape is unmistakable.
funFacts: Before baking, a pretzel takes a short bath in lye, which is what gives it the dark, shiny crust.
The Bavarian Breze has been registered as a protected geographical indication since 2014.
Philadelphia counts as the pretzel capital of the US, where people eat many times the national average.

fun_gummy_bear_day.intro: A day for the chewiest bears in the world. Gummi bears started out in a German kitchen and now come in every colour, flavour and questionable shape imaginable.
funFacts: Hans Riegel invented the gummi bear in Bonn in 1922; the original Tanzbär was taller and slimmer than today's version.
The brand name HARIBO is simply short for Hans Riegel Bonn.
Classic gummi bears are made mostly of glucose syrup, sugar and gelatine, which gives them their bounce.

fun_superhero_day.intro: Capes, masks and impossible landings: a day for comic-book heroes and for the everyday people we quietly call heroes too.
funFacts: Superman appeared in Action Comics #1 in 1938 and is regarded as the first modern superhero.
Wonder Woman followed in 1941, created by psychologist William Moulton Marston, co-inventor of an early lie detector.
The trademark on the term Super Hero was held jointly by Marvel and DC for decades, an unusual arrangement between rivals.

fun_international_dance_day.intro: Ballet, breakdance, tango or kitchen disco: the day celebrates every form of dance and opens studios and stages to anyone willing to move.
funFacts: The date honours Jean-Georges Noverre, born on 29 April 1727 and the great reformer of ballet.
The International Theatre Institute launched the day in 1982, and each year a dance figure writes the official message.
The waltz was considered scandalous around 1800 because the couples held each other so closely while turning.

fun_international_jazz_day.intro: The last day of April belongs to jazz: clubs, schools and orchestras around the world play together, improvise and close Jazz Appreciation Month in style.
funFacts: UNESCO proclaimed the day in 2011, and pianist Herbie Hancock hosted the first edition in 2012.
Well over 100 countries take part, with a global concert staged in a different host city each year.
Jazz is usually traced to New Orleans around 1900, where blues, ragtime and brass bands came together.

fun_lei_day.intro: Hawaii's flowery answer to the first of May: people string, wear and give away leis, and the whole day smells of plumeria. A garland says hello, goodbye, congratulations and thank you all at once.
funFacts: Writer Don Blanding suggested a lei holiday in 1928; Grace Tower Warren added the slogan 'May Day is Lei Day'.
Every Hawaiian island has its own lei colour and plant, from Oahu's golden ilima to Kauai's purple mokihana berries.
Leis are woven, braided or strung with a needle, and are traditionally returned to nature rather than thrown in the bin.

fun_ukulele_day.intro: Four nylon strings, a body the size of a shoebox and almost no way to sound gloomy. Today the idea is simply to pick one up and strum, whether you know three chords or thirty.
funFacts: The ukulele grew up in 1880s Hawaii out of the machete, a small guitar brought over by cabinet makers from Madeira.
The Hawaiian name roughly translates as 'jumping flea', said to describe the way a player's fingers dart about.
A standard ukulele is tuned G-C-E-A, and its top string sits higher in pitch than the one below it.

fun_two_different_colored_shoes_day.intro: Wear one red shoe and one blue one and see who notices. A tiny, harmless act of rebellion against the idea that everything has to match.
funFacts: The oldest known leather shoe, found in a cave at Areni in Armenia, is roughly 5,500 years old.
Ötzi the Iceman walked in shoes of deer and bear hide, insulated with grass stuffed between the layers.
Shoes shaped separately for left and right feet only became normal in the 19th century; before that many were 'straights'.

fun_star_wars_day.intro: 'May the Fourth be with you' — one pun turned a date into a global fan holiday. Marathons, costumes and lightsaber duels in living rooms everywhere.
funFacts: One early well-known use of the pun was a 1979 newspaper advert congratulating Margaret Thatcher on her election win.
Disney has officially marked the day since 2013, often using it to launch new Star Wars releases.
Fans follow it up with 'Revenge of the Fifth' on 5 May, a day for the villains of the saga.

fun_cartoonists_day.intro: A tip of the hat to the people who can tell a whole story in three panels. Newspaper strips, cartoons and comic books all started with someone at a desk with a pen.
funFacts: Richard F. Outcault's Yellow Kid, from 1895, is one of the first newspaper comic characters — and gave the 'yellow press' its name.
Charles M. Schulz drew nearly 18,000 Peanuts strips over almost 50 years, every single one by his own hand.
Rube Goldberg, whose name now means any absurdly complicated machine, won a Pulitzer Prize for cartooning in 1948.

fun_crepe_suzette_day.intro: Thin pancakes, warm orange butter, a splash of liqueur and a brief burst of flame at the table. Dessert as a small piece of theatre.
funFacts: The sauce is built from butter, sugar, orange juice and zest, then flambéed with an orange liqueur such as Grand Marnier.
Legend credits a teenage waiter in 1890s Monte Carlo with setting the sauce alight by accident; food historians are sceptical.
Crêpes are poured so thin that a good cook can spread the batter across the pan in a single wrist movement.

fun_mural_day.intro: A day for the art you cannot hang on a wall, because it is the wall. Murals turn blank walls, underpasses and gable ends into something worth looking up at.
funFacts: Mexican muralism made the form famous in the 1920s, with Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painting public buildings.
Berlin's East Side Gallery stretches 1,316 metres along a surviving stretch of the Wall and is one of the longest open-air galleries.
Painting on walls is the oldest art we know: the cave images at Lascaux are roughly 17,000 years old.

fun_world_donkey_day.intro: A day for the patient, long-eared workmate that has carried people and their luggage for thousands of years — and is usually far cleverer than its reputation suggests.
funFacts: Donkeys were domesticated in north-east Africa some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, most likely by herding peoples in Nubia.
A donkey's bray carries for more than three kilometres, handy for keeping in touch across open desert country.
What looks like stubbornness is caution: a donkey stops to think about danger instead of bolting the way a horse does.

fun_lost_sock_memorial_day.intro: A cheerfully silly farewell to every sock that went into the wash as one of a pair and came out alone. Time to let the survivor go, or give it a mismatched new life.
funFacts: The word sock comes from the Latin soccus, a light slipper worn by comic actors on the Roman stage.
Knitted Egyptian socks with a split toe, made to be worn with sandals, survive from roughly 300-500 AD.
William Lee invented the stocking frame in 1589 — the first knitting machine, built specifically to make socks faster.

fun_shrimp_day.intro: Grilled, fried, in a curry or straight from the pan with garlic: shrimp are one of the fastest routes from kitchen to table. A day to enjoy them without ceremony.
funFacts: Shrimp turn pink when cooked because heat frees the pigment astaxanthin from the proteins that were hiding it.
The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast that the collapsing bubble makes one of the loudest sounds in the ocean.
Cleaner shrimp run 'cleaning stations' on reefs where fish line up to have parasites picked off.

fun_twilight_zone_day.intro: A day for the anthology series that made the twist ending famous. Half an hour, one strange idea, and a closing line that leaves you staring at the ceiling.
funFacts: Rod Serling created the show and wrote or co-wrote 92 of its 156 episodes between 1959 and 1964.
He chose science fiction partly because network censors let him say things there that a realistic drama could not.
The phrase 'the twilight zone' left the screen and became everyday shorthand for anything unsettlingly odd.

fun_limerick_day.intro: Five lines, a bouncing rhythm, a rhyme scheme of AABBA and a punchline that should really not be taken seriously. Today the challenge is to write one yourself.
funFacts: The date is Edward Lear's birthday: the English writer and illustrator was born on 12 May 1812.
Lear did not invent the limerick, but his 1846 Book of Nonsense made the form famous far beyond Britain.
Lines one, two and five rhyme and are long; lines three and four rhyme with each other and are short.

fun_world_cocktail_day.intro: The birthday of a word: on this date in 1806 a New York paper printed the first known definition of a cocktail. Reason enough to shake, stir and clink a glass.
funFacts: On 13 May 1806 The Balance and Columbian Repository defined a cocktail as spirits, sugar, water and bitters.
That description is essentially the recipe for what we now call an Old Fashioned.
Jerry Thomas published the first proper bartender's guide, How to Mix Drinks, in 1862.

fun_dance_like_a_chicken_day.intro: Beaks, flapping wings, wiggle, four claps — the dance nobody admits to knowing and everybody joins in anyway. A day to give in gracefully.
funFacts: Swiss accordionist Werner Thomas wrote the tune in Davos in the 1950s and called it Der Ententanz, the duck dance.
It became the 'chicken' dance in Tulsa in 1981, when an Oktoberfest could find a chicken costume but no duck one.
More than 140 versions have been recorded, adding up to tens of millions of records pressed worldwide.

fun_chocolate_chip_day.intro: The small brown lumps that turn plain dough into a cookie worth queueing for. Today they get the credit rather than the biscuit around them.
funFacts: Ruth Wakefield of the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts put chopped chocolate into cookie dough in the 1930s.
Nestlé printed her recipe on its chocolate wrappers and began selling ready-made morsels in 1939.
Baking chips hold their shape in the oven because they contain less cocoa butter than a bar of eating chocolate.

fun_international_day_of_light.intro: A UNESCO day for everything light does: sunrise, rainbows, fibre-optic cables and laser surgery. The date marks the moment the laser stopped being theory.
funFacts: On 16 May 1960 Theodore Maiman ran the first working laser, using a synthetic ruby crystal and a flash lamp.
Laser is an acronym: light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.
Sunlight needs about eight minutes and twenty seconds to travel from the Sun to your window.

fun_mushroom_hunting_day.intro: Basket, knife, sturdy boots and a slow walk with your eyes on the forest floor. Mushroom hunting is half a hobby, half a treasure hunt — with a strict rule about never eating anything you cannot name.
funFacts: Fungi are their own kingdom, and genetically they sit closer to animals than to plants.
The mushroom you pick is only the fruiting body; the actual organism is a web of threads spread through the soil.
One honey fungus in Oregon covers several square kilometres and counts as one of the largest organisms on Earth.

fun_international_museum_day.intro: Thousands of museums open their doors with special tours, late openings and free entry. A day to walk into the building you always mean to visit.
funFacts: The International Council of Museums has coordinated the day since 1977, each year under a new theme.
By 2017 some 36,000 museums in 156 countries were taking part.
The Ashmolean in Oxford, opened in 1683, is often called the first university museum open to the public.

fun_devils_food_cake_day.intro: Dark, damp and unapologetically chocolatey — the wicked twin of the pale, airy angel food cake. A day for a very large slice.
funFacts: Recipes under the name devil's food appear in American cookbooks from around the turn of the twentieth century.
The name is a joke about its opposite: angel food cake is white, fat-free and feather-light.
Natural cocoa reacting with baking soda can give the crumb a reddish tint — the same effect behind red velvet cake.

fun_world_bee_day.intro: A UN day for the small striped workers behind a huge share of what ends up on our plates. Beekeepers open hives, schools plant flowers, and honey gets eaten.
funFacts: The date honours Anton Janša, a pioneer of modern beekeeping, baptised in Slovenia on 20 May 1734.
Karl von Frisch decoded the waggle dance, which tells hive mates the direction and distance of food, and shared a Nobel Prize in 1973.
One worker bee produces roughly a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire life.

fun_international_tea_day.intro: A UN day for the world's second-most-drunk liquid after plain water. Green, black, oolong or white — all of it starts on the same bush.
funFacts: Green, oolong and black tea all come from Camellia sinensis; only the degree of oxidation differs.
Chinese legend credits the mythical emperor Shennong with discovering tea in 2737 BC.
Turkey drinks more tea per person than anywhere else, well ahead of the countries usually associated with the habit.

fun_world_goth_day.intro: Black lace, dry humour and a soundtrack of guitars in minor keys. A day for a subculture that has been cheerfully misunderstood for forty years.
funFacts: The day began in the UK in 2009, sparked by a BBC Radio 6 Music week devoted to musical subcultures.
Bauhaus's 1979 single Bela Lugosi's Dead is widely treated as the starting pistol for gothic rock.
Leipzig's Wave-Gotik-Treffen draws tens of thousands of visitors and turns the whole city black each spring.

fun_world_turtle_day.intro: A day for one of the calmest designs in the animal kingdom: an animal that carries its own house and is in absolutely no hurry.
funFacts: The shell is not a shed-able case: the upper part is fused with the turtle's spine and ribs.
In many species the nest temperature decides whether the hatchlings are male or female.
Turtles have been around since the Triassic, which makes their lineage well over 200 million years old.

fun_escargot_day.intro: Snails baked in garlic and parsley butter, eaten with special tongs and a tiny fork. Strange the first time, hard to give up afterwards.
funFacts: The classic Burgundy version uses Helix pomatia and a butter beaten together with garlic, parsley and shallots.
The dish has its own cutlery: a dimpled plate, spring-loaded tongs and a narrow two-pronged fork.
A snail eats with a radula, a rasping tongue carrying thousands of microscopic teeth.

fun_towel_day.intro: Fans of Douglas Adams carry a towel around all day, because the Hitchhiker's Guide insists it is the most massively useful thing an interstellar traveller can own.
funFacts: The first Towel Day was held on 25 May 2001, two weeks after Douglas Adams died.
In the books, anyone still holding their towel is assumed to have their whole life under control.
Astronauts Samantha Cristoforetti and Tim Peake have both celebrated the day aboard the International Space Station.

fun_world_dracula_day.intro: The anniversary of the novel that gave the world its most famous vampire. A day for capes, castles and reading by candlelight.
funFacts: Bram Stoker's Dracula went on sale in London in late May 1897, bound in yellow cloth with red lettering.
The manuscript carried the working title The Un-Dead until shortly before publication.
The book is told entirely through diary entries, letters, newspaper cuttings and a ship's log.

fun_grape_popsicle_day.intro: Purple, sticky, gone in five minutes and guaranteed to stain your tongue. The ice lolly is summer's cheapest pleasure, and today it gets its own date.
funFacts: Eleven-year-old Frank Epperson left a drink with a stirring stick outside overnight in 1905 and found it frozen solid.
He patented the frozen treat in 1924, almost twenty years after that accident.
He called it an Epsicle; his children insisted on "Pop's sicle", and the shorter name stuck.

fun_hamburger_day.intro: Bun, patty, whatever you like in between. Few dishes have travelled further or been argued about more, and today the only job is to eat one.
funFacts: The name travels back to Hamburg via the 'Hamburg steak' that German emigrants took to the United States.
Several American towns claim to have served the first burger in a bun, and none of them can prove it.
The 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis is often credited with introducing the sandwich to a mass audience.

fun_paperclip_day.intro: A bent piece of wire that has outlasted almost every office gadget invented since. Cheap, silent, endlessly reusable — and quietly heroic.
funFacts: The familiar double-oval Gem clip was never patented; it simply appeared in Britain in the late 19th century.
Norwegian Johan Vaaler patented a wire clip in 1899, though his design lacked the Gem's two full loops.
Under German occupation, Norwegians wore paperclips on their lapels as a silent sign of solidarity.

fun_potato_day.intro: A UN day for the lumpy, unglamorous tuber that feeds more people than almost anything else. Boiled, mashed, roasted or fried — nobody agrees which is best.
funFacts: The potato was domesticated in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago and reached Europe in the 16th century.
Peru alone holds thousands of native varieties, in colours ranging from cream to deep purple.
Potatoes were grown aboard a Space Shuttle mission in 1995, one of the first food crops cultivated in orbit.

fun_world_parrot_day.intro: Loud, brilliantly coloured and far too clever for their own good. A day for the birds that will happily outlive, outwit and out-argue their owners.
funFacts: The day was launched by the World Parrot Trust in 2004.
Parrots do not have vocal cords; they shape sounds with the syrinx and a remarkably muscular tongue.
Alex, an African grey studied by Irene Pepperberg, learned to use more than a hundred words meaningfully.

fun_dinosaur_day.intro: A day for the giants that ruled the planet long before us. Museums, model kits and children who can pronounce Parasaurolophus faster than any adult all get their moment.
funFacts: Richard Owen coined the word dinosaur in 1842 from Greek roots meaning roughly terrible or fearfully great lizard.
Birds are living dinosaurs: they descend from small feathered theropods, so a sparrow is closer kin to T. rex than any lizard.
More time separates Stegosaurus from Tyrannosaurus rex than separates T. rex from us.

fun_rocky_road_day.intro: Chocolate ice cream with marshmallows and nuts in it: rocky road is the flavour that refuses to be smooth. A day to order the scoop with the most texture.
funFacts: Ice cream maker William Dreyer is credited with the flavour in 1929, reportedly cutting marshmallows with his wife's sewing scissors.
In Australia and Britain rocky road is not ice cream at all but a chilled chocolate bar full of marshmallow and nuts.
Marshmallows once really did contain marsh mallow: the root sap of Althaea officinalis was whipped with sugar.

fun_world_bicycle_day.intro: Two wheels, no fuel, and the same basic shape for over a century. This day celebrates the most efficient machine ever built for moving a human being.
funFacts: The UN General Assembly declared 3 June World Bicycle Day in April 2018.
Karl Drais rode his Laufmaschine near Mannheim in 1817, the pedal-free ancestor of every bicycle since.
The Netherlands has more bicycles than people, with well over 20 million bikes for around 18 million inhabitants.

fun_cheese_day.intro: Fresh, blue, hard, runny or grilled: cheese is milk that learned to keep. A day to build a cheese board and eat the crumbs off the paper.
funFacts: It takes roughly ten litres of milk to make one kilogram of hard cheese.
The holes in Emmental are gas bubbles: propionic acid bacteria give off carbon dioxide as the wheel ripens.
Traces of cheese-making were found on 7,000-year-old pottery sieves from Poland, some of the oldest evidence known.

fun_gingerbread_day.intro: Gingerbread is not just for December. This day puts the spiced dough back on the table in the middle of summer, whether as a soft cookie or a crisp little house.
funFacts: Nuremberg has been famous for Lebkuchen since the Middle Ages, helped by its position on the spice trade routes.
Gingerbread men are traditionally credited to the court of Elizabeth I, who had them baked in the likeness of guests.
The heat in ginger comes from gingerol, a chemical relative of the compounds that make chilli and pepper sharp.

fun_yo_yo_day.intro: A disc, an axle and a string. The yo-yo has been going up and down for over two thousand years and still turns up in every school playground.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Donald F. Duncan, the businessman who turned the yo-yo into an American craze in the 1930s.
A Greek vase from around 440 BC shows a boy playing with a disc toy that looks remarkably like a yo-yo.
In 1985 a yo-yo flew aboard Space Shuttle Discovery so astronauts could film how it behaves without gravity.

fun_chocolate_ice_cream_day.intro: Vanilla may be the bestseller, but chocolate came first. A day for the darkest scoop in the freezer, in a cone, a cup or straight from the tub.
funFacts: A Neapolitan recipe collection from 1692 already described frozen chocolate, decades before vanilla ice cream was written down.
Cocoa pods grow straight out of the trunk of the cacao tree, a growth habit botanists call cauliflory.
Good ice cream is mostly about small ice crystals, which is why the mixture has to be churned while it freezes.

fun_best_friends_day.intro: The person who knows your worst stories and stays anyway. This day is a nudge to actually call them instead of just thinking about it.
funFacts: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar suggests we manage around 150 stable relationships, but only about five truly close ones.
Merriam-Webster added the abbreviation BFF to its dictionary in 2010, decades after teenagers invented it.
Knotted friendship bracelets come from Central and South American macramé traditions and spread worldwide in the 1980s.

fun_donald_duck_day.intro: Sailor shirt, no trousers, and a temper that never lasts long. This day marks the screen debut of the most famous duck in the world.
funFacts: Donald first appeared on 9 June 1934 in the Silly Symphony short The Wise Little Hen.
Clarence Nash created the squawking voice and kept performing it for around fifty years.
German readers know him through Erika Fuchs, whose witty translations put words like seufz and ächz into everyday language.

fun_world_art_nouveau_day.intro: Curving iron, whiplash lines and flowers growing across facades: a day for the style that briefly turned whole cities into ornament, from Barcelona to Brussels to Riga.
funFacts: The date marks the death day of two masters of the style, Antoni Gaudí and the Hungarian architect Ödön Lechner.
The same movement has a different name almost everywhere: Jugendstil in Germany, Modernisme in Catalonia, Secession in Vienna.
Hector Guimard's cast-iron Paris Métro entrances from around 1900 are among the most photographed pieces of the style.

fun_corn_on_the_cob_day.intro: Corn eaten the honest way: straight off the cob, with butter running down your wrists and a row of stripped cobs piling up on the plate. Grill it, boil it, salt it, repeat.
funFacts: The rows of kernels on a cob are almost always an even number, because the florets that become kernels develop in neat pairs.
Every silk thread leads to exactly one kernel and has to catch pollen; the gaps on a cob are the silks that missed out.
Maize was domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from teosinte, a grass carrying a handful of rock-hard seeds.

fun_red_rose_day.intro: One flower says more than most sentences. This day belongs to the red rose, in the garden, on the table or handed over without much explanation.
funFacts: Roses have been cultivated for around 5,000 years, and fossil roses are some 35 million years old.
It takes several tonnes of petals to distil a single kilogram of rose oil, which is why the essence costs more than gold by weight.
The Victorian language of flowers pinned each colour to a message, and red was reserved for declared love.

fun_sewing_machine_day.intro: The machine that took clothing out of the hand-stitched era. A day for the quiet workhorse in the cupboard and everyone who still repairs instead of replaces.
funFacts: Elias Howe patented a lockstitch machine in 1846, and Isaac Singer's marketing turned it into a household object.
Barthélemy Thimonnier's Paris sewing workshop was wrecked in 1831 by tailors who feared for their livelihoods.
A lockstitch needs two threads: the needle thread from above and the bobbin thread hidden underneath.

fun_strawberry_shortcake_day.intro: Sweet biscuit, sliced strawberries, a cloud of whipped cream. The dessert that marks the start of proper summer, best eaten outdoors.
funFacts: Strawberries are not botanically berries: the tiny pips on the outside are the real fruits, and there are around 200 per strawberry.
The garden strawberry is a hybrid, bred in Brittany around 1750 from a Chilean and a North American species.
In the American original the shortcake is a crumbly biscuit, not the sponge base sold in Europe.

fun_lobster_day.intro: Once so common it was fed to prisoners, now the centrepiece of the menu. A day for the armoured crustacean with the outsized claws.
funFacts: In colonial New England lobster was cheap fare for servants and inmates, and contracts limited how often it could be served.
Lobster blood is bluish because it carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.
A live lobster is mottled brown; heat frees the red pigment astaxanthin from its protein and the shell turns scarlet.

fun_bloomsday.intro: Dublin spends this day walking through a novel. Readers in Edwardian dress retrace the route of Leopold Bloom, book in hand, from breakfast to the small hours.
funFacts: The whole of James Joyce's Ulysses takes place on a single day, Thursday 16 June 1904, in Dublin.
Joyce chose the date because it was the day he first walked out with Nora Barnacle, who later became his wife.
The first Bloomsday was staged in 1954 for the fiftieth anniversary, and the pilgrims never made it to the end of the route.

fun_apple_strudel_day.intro: Paper-thin pastry, apples, raisins, cinnamon and a snowfall of icing sugar. A day for the most patient piece of baking in Central European kitchens.
funFacts: The oldest known strudel recipes date from 1696 and survive in a handwritten cookbook kept in Vienna.
The dough is stretched by hand until you can supposedly read a newspaper through it.
Strudel means whirlpool in German, which is exactly what the rolled-up cross-section looks like.

fun_sushi_day.intro: Rice, vinegar, fish and a lot of practice. Sushi travelled from Japanese street stalls to almost every city on earth, and this day toasts the journey.
funFacts: The word sushi refers to the seasoned rice, not the fish on top of it.
Its ancestor narezushi was a preservation method: fish was fermented in rice, and the rice was thrown away.
Nigiri appeared in early 19th-century Edo as fast food sold from stalls, meant to be eaten standing up with your fingers.

fun_world_sauntering_day.intro: Not a run, not a march, not even a brisk walk. Today the correct speed is slow enough to notice things, with no destination worth hurrying towards.
funFacts: The day was dreamed up in 1979 at the Grand Hotel on Mackinac Island as a gentle protest against the jogging boom.
That hotel porch is one of the longest in the world at around 200 metres, which makes it ideal for the purpose.
A popular folk etymology derives saunter from à la Sainte Terre, the stroll of a pilgrim to the Holy Land.

fun_vanilla_milkshake_day.intro: Milk, ice cream, vanilla, and a straw that never quite copes. The plainest milkshake on the menu is still the one most people order twice.
funFacts: In the 1880s a milkshake was an adult drink: eggs, cream and a shot of whisky, shaken by hand.
Vanilla comes from an orchid whose flowers open for a single day and are pollinated by hand almost everywhere.
The technique was worked out by Edmond Albius on Réunion in 1841, when he was still a teenager.

fun_world_music_day.intro: On the longest day of the year, amateurs and professionals play for free in streets, courtyards and parks. Anyone with an instrument is allowed on stage, because there is no stage.
funFacts: The Fête de la Musique started in Paris in 1982, launched by culture minister Jack Lang and Maurice Fleuret.
The French name is a pun: fête de la musique sounds like faites de la musique, meaning make music.
It is now celebrated in around 120 countries; Berlin has held its own edition since 1995.

fun_onion_ring_day.intro: A slice of onion, a jacket of batter, hot oil and nothing else. The side order that quietly steals attention from whatever it was ordered with.
funFacts: John Mollard's cookbook of 1802 already describes onion rings dipped in batter and fried, long before diners existed.
Onions make you cry because cutting releases an enzyme that produces the irritant syn-propanethial-S-oxide.
Chilling the onion first slows that reaction down, which is why a cold onion is a kinder onion.

fun_olympic_day.intro: A day when clubs, schools and cities put on runs and open training sessions for anyone who turns up. The Olympic idea, minus the qualifying times.
funFacts: The date marks the founding of the International Olympic Committee at the Sorbonne in Paris on 23 June 1894.
The first Olympic Day was held in 1948 in nine countries, from Portugal and Greece to Uruguay and Canada.
The Olympic Day Run followed in 1987 and is now open to anyone, whatever their pace.

fun_international_fairy_day.intro: Tiny doors at the foot of trees, glitter in the garden and stories that stay deliberately unproven. A day for the small folk of European folklore.
funFacts: The Cottingley Fairies photographs of 1917 convinced Arthur Conan Doyle; the cousins admitted the cut-out hoax only in 1983.
Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream gave the fairy world its best-known cast: Titania, Oberon and Puck.
Fairy rings of mushrooms are real: a fungus spreads outwards underground and fruits along the growing edge.

fun_global_beatles_day.intro: Four musicians from Liverpool, roughly ten years of recording, and a shadow over popular music ever since. A day to play the albums loudly and in order.
funFacts: The date recalls 25 June 1967, when the band played All You Need Is Love live on the first worldwide satellite broadcast.
That programme, Our World, reached an estimated 400 to 700 million viewers, the largest television audience up to then.
The zebra crossing from the Abbey Road cover was given listed heritage status in 2010.

fun_chocolate_pudding_day.intro: Warm from the pan or cold from the fridge, chocolate pudding is a dessert with no ambition beyond being brown, sweet and spoonable. A day to eat it straight out of the bowl.
funFacts: The word pudding comes from the French boudin and once meant a stuffed, sausage-like dish; the sweet career came much later.
Linnaeus named the cacao tree Theobroma cacao in 1753, from the Greek for food of the gods.
The skin on cooled pudding is milk protein drying at the surface; press cling film onto it while hot and no skin forms.

fun_sunglasses_day.intro: Half eye protection, half disguise. On the shortest nights of the year, sunglasses get their own day, whether on the nose or pushed into the hair.
funFacts: Inuit peoples carved slitted snow goggles from bone or antler long before glass lenses existed.
Chinese judges are said to have used smoke-coloured quartz lenses to keep their expressions unreadable in court.
Polarised lenses arrived in 1936, when Edwin Land applied his Polaroid filter material to sunglasses.

fun_tau_day.intro: A quietly rebellious day for anyone who thinks the circle constant should be 6.28, not 3.14. Tradition demands twice as much pie as on Pi Day.
funFacts: Tau is defined as two pi, roughly 6.28, which is why the date falls on 6/28.
A full turn is one tau in radians, so a quarter circle is simply tau over four instead of pi over two.
The idea gained followers through Bob Palais' 2001 article Pi Is Wrong and Michael Hartl's Tau Manifesto of 2010.

fun_camera_day.intro: From a wooden box with a brass lens to the thing in your pocket. A day for photography and for the boxes of old prints nobody can throw away.
funFacts: The camera obscura was described in detail around 1020 by the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, centuries before film.
The oldest surviving photograph, Nicéphore Niépce's view from a window, needed an exposure of many hours.
Oskar Barnack's Leica of 1925 made 35 mm film the standard and let photographers work handheld.

fun_meteor_watch_day.intro: No telescope, no app, no ticket: just a dark patch of sky, a blanket and the patience to keep looking up. Sooner or later something bright scratches across the dark.
funFacts: It is a meteoroid out in space, a meteor while it glows, and a meteorite only once a piece actually lands.
Most shooting stars burn up more than 80 kilometres up, and about 15,000 tonnes of space material reach the atmosphere each year.
The Perseids peak around 12 August; the dust comes from comet Swift-Tuttle, which passes by only every 133 years.

fun_july_morning.intro: A Bulgarian summer ritual: stay up through the short night and greet the very first sunrise of July, ideally with your feet in the sand of the Black Sea coast.
funFacts: The tradition began in 1985 in Varna and now draws thousands to the Black Sea coast and the Danube every 1 July.
Its name comes from 'July Morning', a 1971 song by the British rock band Uriah Heep.
Cape Shabla is Bulgaria's easternmost point, so the sun comes up there before anywhere else in the country.

fun_world_ufo_day.intro: An evening for looking up. Sky-watchers gather on 2 July, the date of the alleged 1947 crash near Roswell, to swap stories about lights that nobody can quite explain.
funFacts: The US Air Force later put the Roswell debris down to a balloon from the secret Project Mogul, which listened for Soviet nuclear tests.
Some people mark the day on 24 June instead, when pilot Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting gave the world the phrase 'flying saucer'.
Officials have largely dropped 'UFO': since 2022 the term of choice in the US is UAP, unidentified anomalous phenomena.

fun_eat_beans_day.intro: A cheerful nudge towards the most underrated thing in the cupboard. Beans are cheap, filling and turn up in almost every cuisine on earth.
funFacts: Beans host rhizobia bacteria in their root nodules that pull nitrogen out of the air, leaving the soil richer than they found it.
Heinz baked beans first reached Britain in 1886 as an imported delicacy sold at Fortnum & Mason.
Raw or undercooked kidney beans can cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea. Proper boiling inactivates their harmful lectin.

fun_alice_in_wonderland_day.intro: On this date in 1862 a boat trip near Oxford turned into one of the strangest and best-loved stories ever told. A good day for tea parties and impossible logic.
funFacts: On 4 July 1862 Lewis Carroll rowed up the Isis with the three Liddell sisters and invented the tale to pass the time.
Alice Liddell was ten years old on that trip, and it was she who asked Carroll to write the story down.
The book has never been out of print and has been translated into 174 languages.

fun_mechanical_pencil_day.intro: A small salute to the pencil that never needs sharpening. Click, and there is a fresh millimetre of lead waiting for you.
funFacts: The first patent for a refillable pencil with a lead-propelling mechanism went to Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in Britain in 1822.
The oldest known example was recovered from the wreck of HMS Pandora, which sank in 1791.
Pencil lead has never contained lead: it is a mix of graphite and clay, and more clay means a harder, lighter line.

fun_international_kissing_day.intro: A reminder that a kiss costs nothing and is worth a great deal. The day took shape in Britain in the 1990s and has been happily copied ever since.
funFacts: Kissing has its own field of research with a suitably serious name: philematology.
The longest kiss on record lasted more than 58 hours, set by a Thai couple in Pattaya in 2013.
Latin had three separate words for it: osculum for friendship, basium for affection and savium for passion.

fun_world_chocolate_day.intro: One day a year when nobody has to justify the second piece. Dark, milk or white, chocolate is the closest thing the world has to a universal treat.
funFacts: Cacao beans once worked as money: the Aztecs used them to pay tribute and to buy everyday goods.
For most of its history chocolate was a drink; the first bar you could bite came from J. S. Fry & Sons in Bristol in 1847.
White chocolate contains cocoa butter but no cocoa solids, which is exactly why it never turns brown.

fun_video_game_day.intro: Controllers out. A day for the pixels of your childhood, the co-op sessions on the sofa and that one level you still have not finished.
funFacts: One of the earliest video games, 'Tennis for Two', ran on an oscilloscope built by physicist William Higinbotham in 1958.
An early Pong machine reportedly stopped working because its coin box was jammed completely full of quarters.
Nintendo was founded in 1889 and spent its first decades making hanafuda playing cards.

fun_sugar_cookie_day.intro: Butter, sugar, flour, a cookie cutter. The sugar cookie is deliberately plain so that the icing, the sprinkles and the shape can do the talking.
funFacts: The recipe is traced to German Protestant settlers in Nazareth, Pennsylvania, in the 18th century.
Pennsylvania liked it enough to make the Nazareth sugar cookie its official state cookie in 2001.
Sugar only became an everyday ingredient in Europe after Franz Karl Achard opened the first beet sugar factory in 1801.

fun_pina_colada_day.intro: Pineapple, coconut cream, rum and a lot of ice. The piña colada tastes like a holiday even when you are drinking it on a rainy Tuesday.
funFacts: Puerto Rico made the piña colada its official national drink in 1978.
The Caribe Hilton in San Juan claims its bartender Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero mixed the first one in 1954.
The name is simply Spanish for 'strained pineapple'.

fun_bandoneon_day.intro: Argentina celebrates the wheezing, sighing box that gives tango its voice. It is held between both hands and played by pushing and pulling the bellows.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Aníbal Troilo, born on 11 July 1914 and still the most famous bandoneonist of all.
The instrument is German: it is named after the Krefeld music dealer Heinrich Band and was first meant for church and popular tunes.
Bandoneons were never mass-produced in Argentina, and German production stopped around the Second World War, so old instruments are rare and pricey.

fun_etch_a_sketch_day.intro: Two knobs, one line, no undo button. The red drawing toy has been frustrating and delighting people in equal measure since this date in 1960.
funFacts: It went on sale on 12 July 1960 for $2.99 and has since sold more than 100 million units worldwide.
It was invented in France by the electrician André Cassagnes and manufactured by the Ohio Art Company in the US.
The screen is coated on the inside with aluminium powder; the stylus scrapes it away and a good shake puts it back.

fun_embrace_your_geekness_day.intro: Permission, officially granted, to be enthusiastic in public about the thing you know far too much about. Comics, trains, spreadsheets, dinosaurs: all welcome.
funFacts: 'Geek' started out as a fairground word for a sideshow performer before it came to mean a devoted specialist.
'Nerd' first appeared in print in Dr. Seuss's 1950 picture book 'If I Ran the Zoo'.
The first San Diego Comic-Con in 1970 drew a few hundred visitors; today it fills the city with well over 100,000.

fun_world_chimpanzee_day.intro: A day for our closest living relatives, marking the date Jane Goodall first walked into the forest at Gombe and started watching chimpanzees properly.
funFacts: Goodall arrived at Gombe Stream in Tanzania on 14 July 1960; the day has been celebrated since 2018.
She watched chimps strip leaves off twigs to fish termites out of a mound, the first record of a non-human animal making a tool.
Chimpanzees share roughly 99 percent of their DNA with us and greet each other with hugs, kisses and back pats.

fun_tapioca_pudding_day.intro: Small translucent pearls that go delightfully chewy when cooked. Tapioca has been comfort food for generations and, more recently, the best part of bubble tea.
funFacts: Tapioca is pure starch washed out of the cassava root, a staple crop for hundreds of millions of people in the tropics.
Raw cassava is toxic and has to be processed first; the washed-out starch itself is perfectly harmless.
The chewy black pearls in bubble tea are tapioca too, a Taiwanese invention from the 1980s.

fun_world_snake_day.intro: A day for the most misunderstood animals in the garden. Snakes have no legs, no eyelids and no external ears, and still manage to live almost everywhere on earth.
funFacts: There are more than 3,000 snake species; only about 200 of them are considered dangerous to humans.
Snakes cannot blink: a clear scale called the brille covers each eye and is shed along with the skin.
They smell with their tongue, which carries scent particles to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth.

fun_world_emoji_day.intro: The day the little yellow faces get their own party. Look at the calendar emoji on your phone and you will see exactly why 17 July was chosen.
funFacts: The date comes from the calendar emoji, which shows 17 July on Apple devices — the day iCal was announced in 2002.
World Emoji Day was launched in 2014 by Jeremy Burge, the founder of Emojipedia.
In 2015 Oxford Dictionaries picked the 'face with tears of joy' as word of the year, the first time a pictograph won.

fun_world_listening_day.intro: An invitation to stop talking for a moment and pay attention to how the world actually sounds — the birds, the traffic, the hum of your own kitchen.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Canadian composer R. Murray Schafer, born on 18 July 1933, who popularised the idea of the soundscape.
The World Listening Project started the day in 2010; people mark it with listening walks and field recordings.
In the world's quietest rooms, anechoic chambers, sound levels drop below zero decibels and you can hear your own blood.

fun_palace_day.intro: Europe's royal residences open their archives and their side doors online, sharing the stories, staircases and quirks that visitors usually walk straight past.
funFacts: The Network of European Royal Residences launched #PalaceDay in 2016; every year has a different theme.
The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles is about 73 metres long and lined with 357 mirrors.
Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna has 1,441 rooms, of which only around 40 are open to visitors.

fun_international_chess_day.intro: Sixty-four squares, thirty-two pieces and more possible games than there are atoms in the observable universe. Time to challenge someone.
funFacts: The date marks the founding of the world chess federation FIDE in Paris on 20 July 1924; the UN recognised the day in 2019.
Castling moves the king and a rook in a single turn.
Chess grew out of the Indian game chaturanga, played from around the 6th century onwards.

fun_junk_food_day.intro: One day off from the good intentions. Burgers, crisps, gummy sweets — whatever it is you pretend not to eat, today it goes on the plate without comment.
funFacts: The term 'junk food' was popularised in the 1970s, notably by nutrition campaigner Michael Jacobson in 1972.
Legend has it the potato crisp was born in Saratoga Springs in 1853, when a cook sliced potatoes wafer-thin for a fussy guest.
US surveys found that on any given day about a third of adults eat fast food.

fun_hammock_day.intro: The world's most persuasive argument for doing nothing. Two trees, a length of cloth, and the afternoon takes care of itself.
funFacts: The word travelled into English via the Spanish hamaca from the Taíno language of the Caribbean.
Sailors slept in hammocks below deck for centuries because they swing with the roll of the ship instead of against it.
From Apollo 12 onwards, astronauts slept in hammocks strung inside the lunar module.

fun_vanilla_ice_cream_day.intro: The flavour everyone calls plain and everyone keeps ordering. Real vanilla ice cream is anything but boring — it starts with the pod of an orchid.
funFacts: Vanilla comes from an orchid, and outside its Mexican home every flower has to be pollinated by hand.
The hand-pollination trick was worked out in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old on the island of Réunion.
Thomas Jefferson's handwritten vanilla ice cream recipe is kept in the Library of Congress.

fun_tequila_day.intro: A toast to the spirit of the blue agave. Sipped slowly rather than knocked back, good tequila tastes of pepper, earth and roasted plant hearts.
funFacts: Tequila may only be made from blue agave and only in defined regions of Mexico, above all the state of Jalisco.
The agave landscape around the town of Tequila has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006.
An agave grows for six to ten years before its heart, the piña, is cut out; it often weighs more than 40 kilograms.

fun_carousel_day.intro: Painted horses, a brass pole and an organ playing slightly out of tune. The carousel is the one fairground ride that works just as well at three as at eighty-three.
funFacts: On 25 July 1871 William Schneider of Davenport, Iowa was granted the first American carousel patent.
The name comes from the Italian carosello, a horseback game that knights used as riding practice.
European carousels usually turn clockwise, American ones the other way, so riders can grab the brass ring with the right hand.

fun_esperanto_day.intro: The birthday of a language built on purpose to be easy and neutral. Speakers around the world mark the day the very first Esperanto textbook appeared.
funFacts: On 26 July 1887 L. L. Zamenhof published the Unua Libro, the first textbook of the language.
He signed it 'Doktoro Esperanto', meaning 'one who hopes' — and the pseudonym became the name of the language.
Esperanto has sixteen grammatical rules, no irregular verbs, and a small number of native speakers who grew up with it at home.

fun_sleepy_head_day.intro: Finland's revenge on late risers. Whoever is still in bed gets woken with water — and in one town a well-known guest ends up in the sea before breakfast.
funFacts: In Naantali a Finnish celebrity is thrown into the harbour at 7 a.m.; who it will be is kept secret until the moment itself.
The custom goes back to the Middle Ages, when the last sleeper in the house was thought to be lazy for the rest of the year.
Every mayor of Naantali has taken the plunge at least once.

fun_singing_telegram_day.intro: The day a telegram learned to sing. Instead of the usual bad news, a Western Union operator delivered a birthday greeting down the telephone — in tune.
funFacts: On 28 July 1933 operator Lucille Lipps sang a birthday message to the singer Rudy Vallée, the first singing telegram.
It was the idea of PR man George P. Oslin, who was told he was making a laughing stock of the company.
Western Union finally shut down its telegram service in 2006, after more than 150 years.

fun_chicken_wing_day.intro: Sticky fingers, a pile of napkins and a bowl of blue cheese dip. The chicken wing went from kitchen scrap to bar-food royalty in a single generation.
funFacts: In 1977 the city of Buffalo declared 29 July Chicken Wing Day, honouring Anchor Bar co-owner Frank Bellissimo.
Buffalo wings are said to have been invented at that bar in 1964; before then wings mostly ended up in the stockpot.
Buffalo, New York holds an annual wing festival whose hall of fame is called the Hall of Flame.

fun_paperback_book_day.intro: The day good books stopped being expensive. Ten cheap little volumes went on sale in 1935 and changed who was allowed to own a library.
funFacts: On 30 July 1935 Penguin published its first ten paperbacks at sixpence each — the price of a packet of cigarettes.
Allen Lane had the idea after finding nothing worth reading at a railway station bookstall; Woolworths took the first big order.
The covers were colour-coded: orange for fiction, green for crime, dark blue for biography.

fun_raspberry_cake_day.intro: The last day of July, and raspberry season is at its peak. Fold them into a sponge, pile them on cream, or simply eat them off your fingertips.
funFacts: Botanically a raspberry is not a berry at all but an aggregate fruit made of dozens of tiny drupelets.
Raspberries come off their core when picked, which is why they are hollow; blackberries keep theirs.
They belong to the rose family, along with apples, pears, cherries and strawberries.

fun_world_wide_web_day.intro: A nod to the invention that turned a network of computers into something everyone could browse. One day a year to remember that links, pages and bookmarks were once a brand new idea.
funFacts: Tim Berners-Lee wrote his proposal for the web at CERN in March 1989; his boss famously called it 'vague but exciting'.
The first web server was a NeXT computer carrying a handwritten label: 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'
In 1993 CERN put the web software into the public domain, which is why nobody has ever had to pay a licence fee to run a website.

fun_ice_cream_sandwich_day.intro: Ice cream, squeezed between two biscuits, eaten with your fingers. The most portable dessert of the summer gets its own date in the middle of the hottest month.
funFacts: Pushcart vendors in New York were selling ice cream sandwiches for a penny each around 1899.
Australia has its own classic, the vanilla slice between wafers, while San Francisco is proud of its oatmeal-cookie It's-It.
The wafers are baked deliberately soft so your teeth go through them instead of squeezing the ice cream out of the sides.

fun_watermelon_day.intro: The fruit that makes a picnic feel like a picnic. Sticky fingers, a slice the size of your face and a competition over who can spit the seeds furthest.
funFacts: A watermelon is about 92 percent water, which is exactly why it works so well on a hot afternoon.
Botanically it is a berry, a type called a pepo, with a hard rind and a soft fleshy centre.
Japanese growers raise some melons inside glass boxes so they end up square and stack neatly in a fridge.

fun_chocolate_chip_cookie_day.intro: Golden edges, a soft middle and pockets of melting chocolate. A day for the biscuit that nearly every home baker attempts at least once.
funFacts: Ruth Graves Wakefield created the cookie at her Toll House Inn in Massachusetts in the 1930s.
She later let Nestlé print her recipe on their packaging, and the company began selling chocolate in ready-made chips.
Massachusetts made the chocolate chip cookie its official state cookie in 1997 after a campaign by schoolchildren.

fun_traffic_light_day.intro: Red, amber, green: three lamps that quietly organise the whole planet's traffic. A day to appreciate the least glamorous and most useful invention on any street corner.
funFacts: The first electric traffic signal went into service on 5 August 1914 in Cleveland, Ohio, at the corner of Euclid Avenue and East 105th Street.
London had a gas-lit signal outside Parliament back in 1868, but it exploded a year later and injured the constable operating it.
Red means stop because red light scatters least in air and stays visible from the greatest distance in fog and rain.

fun_root_beer_float_day.intro: A scoop of vanilla ice cream dropped into a glass of root beer, and the foam does the rest. Cheap, noisy and wonderfully theatrical.
funFacts: The drink is credited to Frank J. Wisner, who mixed it in Cripple Creek, Colorado, in 1893 and called it a Black Cow.
The foam happens because the ice cream's fat and proteins trap the escaping carbon dioxide in tiny stable bubbles.
Root beer was traditionally flavoured with sassafras root, which US regulators banned as a food additive in 1960.

fun_lighthouse_day.intro: A tip of the cap to the towers that stand in the weather so sailors don't have to guess where the rocks are. Few buildings are as photogenic or as stubborn.
funFacts: The date recalls 7 August 1789, when the US Congress took the country's lighthouses into federal care.
The Pharos of Alexandria was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and stood for roughly 1,500 years.
Augustin-Jean Fresnel's stepped lens of 1822 let a single lamp throw a beam far out to sea instead of wasting it on the sky.

fun_international_cat_day.intro: The day belongs to the housemate who pays no rent, sleeps on the warm laptop and still gets away with everything. Cat people need no further excuse.
funFacts: Cats sleep between twelve and sixteen hours a day, spread over dozens of short naps rather than one long night.
Whiskers are roughly as wide as the cat and work as feelers for judging whether a gap is passable.
Ancient Egypt honoured the cat goddess Bastet, and mummified cats have been found by the thousand at her temple sites.

fun_book_lovers_day.intro: Permission to ignore your inbox, find a quiet corner and read for the pleasure of it. Paper, e-ink or audio, nobody is checking.
funFacts: Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time is often listed as the longest novel ever published, at well over a million words.
The Library of Congress holds around 178 million items and adds thousands more every working day.
Roughly 180 copies of the Gutenberg Bible were printed in the 1450s; about 49 still survive, most of them incomplete.

fun_world_lion_day.intro: A day for the big cat that turns up on coats of arms, football crests and bedtime stories all over the world. Impressive from a safe distance, magnificent in a photograph.
funFacts: A lion's roar can carry about eight kilometres and is used to mark territory and locate the rest of the pride.
Lions are the only cats that live in real social groups; a pride is usually built around related females.
The lionesses do most of the hunting, often in coordinated teams, while the mane mainly signals a male's condition.

fun_hip_hop_day.intro: Turntables, a microphone, a piece of cardboard and a spray can: four elements that grew out of one Bronx party into a global culture. This is the date fans treat as its birthday.
funFacts: On 11 August 1973 DJ Kool Herc played a back-to-school party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, now widely called hip hop's birthplace.
His trick was the break: two copies of the same record, looping the drum passage so dancers never had to stop.
In 2021 the US Senate formally designated 11 August as Hip Hop Celebration Day.

fun_world_elephant_day.intro: The largest land animal on the planet gets a day of its own. Elephants are clever, sociable and, judging by every zoo queue ever, endlessly fascinating to watch.
funFacts: An elephant's trunk contains tens of thousands of muscle units and can both uproot a tree and pick up a single leaf.
Those enormous ears are radiators: blood flowing through them cools down before returning to the body.
Elephant pregnancies last around 22 months, the longest of any land mammal.

fun_lefthanders_day.intro: For everyone who smudges their own handwriting, fights with tin openers and sits at the wrong end of the dinner table. A day to point out that the world is built slightly wrong.
funFacts: Roughly one in ten people is left-handed, and the share is fairly stable across countries and centuries.
The day was first marked in 1976 by Dean R. Campbell, founder of the group Lefthanders International.
Left-handers are unusually successful in fencing, boxing and table tennis, where opponents rarely get to practise against them.

fun_world_lizard_day.intro: Sun-warmed rocks, quick sideways glances and a tail that vanishes round a corner. A day for the reptiles most of us have only ever met on a holiday wall.
funFacts: There are more than 7,000 known lizard species, from thumb-sized geckos to the three-metre Komodo dragon.
Gecko toes are covered in millions of microscopic hairs that grip smooth glass using molecular attraction alone.
Many lizards can shed their tail to escape a predator and grow a replacement, though it is usually shorter and made of cartilage.

fun_relaxation_day.intro: An official excuse to do nothing in particular. No chores, no productivity tips, just a hammock, a bench in the shade or a long afternoon nap.
funFacts: The hammock reached Europe from the Caribbean; the word comes from the Taíno hamaca via Spanish sailors.
Siesta comes from the Latin hora sexta, the sixth hour after sunrise, which is roughly the middle of the day.
Sleep researchers find naps of ten to twenty minutes leave you alert, while longer ones tend to leave you groggy.

fun_roller_coaster_day.intro: The drop, the scream, the wobbly walk back to the exit. A day for the ride that people queue an hour for in order to be terrified for ninety seconds.
funFacts: The date marks 16 August 1898, when Edwin Prescott patented a coaster design with a vertical loop.
The ancestors were the Russian ice slides of the 18th century, wooden hills near St Petersburg covered in ice.
Coney Island's Switchback Railway of 1884 cost five cents and reached a top speed of about ten kilometres per hour.

fun_thrift_shop_day.intro: A day for rummaging: worn-in jackets, odd crockery, a paperback someone loved before you. The joy is in the hunt, and the price tag rarely hurts.
funFacts: Goodwill grew out of a Boston mission founded in 1902, where donated clothes were repaired and resold by the people who needed the work.
The Salvation Army was collecting and reselling household goods through its salvage brigades before 1900.
Wool, cotton and denim all keep their structure for decades, which is why old clothes so often outlast new ones.

fun_bad_poetry_day.intro: Write something dreadful, rhyme moon with spoon and read it aloud without apology. The point is that nobody has to be good at it to enjoy it.
funFacts: William McGonagall of Dundee is routinely called the worst poet in the English language, and his readings drew crowds for exactly that reason.
His Tay Bridge Disaster is still quoted for lines that scan badly and rhyme worse.
Douglas Adams invented Vogon poetry as the third worst in the universe, with an audience tied to uncomfortable chairs.

fun_world_photography_day.intro: From glass plates to the phone in your pocket. A day to notice that we all carry a camera capable of things a 19th-century studio could only dream of.
funFacts: On 19 August 1839 the French government presented the daguerreotype process and declared it free to the world.
The oldest surviving photograph from nature, Nicéphore Niépce's View from the Window at Le Gras, needed an exposure of many hours.
Early portrait sitters used head clamps to stay still, which is part of why nobody in old photographs looks relaxed.

fun_radio_day.intro: The medium that survived television, cassettes and streaming and still keeps people company in the kitchen and the car. A day for crackling frequencies and familiar voices.
funFacts: KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast US election results on 2 November 1920, an event usually called the first commercial radio broadcast.
Marconi reported receiving a signal across the Atlantic in 1901, at a time when physicists doubted radio waves could follow the curve of the Earth.
Orson Welles's 1938 War of the Worlds broadcast is famous less for the panic it caused than for how the story of that panic grew.

fun_spumoni_day.intro: Three coloured layers of Italian ice cream, studded with candied fruit and nuts and cut into slices like a cake. A dessert that arrives looking like a celebration.
funFacts: Spumoni comes from Naples and traditionally combines chocolate, cherry and pistachio layers.
The name is related to spuma, Italian for foam, a nod to how much air is whipped into the cream.
Italian immigrants brought it to the United States in the 19th century, where it became a fixture in Italian-American restaurants.

fun_eat_a_peach_day.intro: Late August is peak peach season, so the instruction is simple: find a ripe one, lean forward and let it drip. Anything else would be a waste.
funFacts: Peaches were domesticated in China thousands of years ago and reached Europe via Persia, which is why the Latin name means Persian apple.
The peach belongs to the rose family and is a close relative of the almond; the kernel inside the stone looks the part.
A nectarine is not a hybrid but a peach with a single gene variant that leaves the skin smooth.

fun_ride_the_wind_day.intro: A day for anything that stays up because the air is moving: gliders, kites, paragliders and the occasional very determined pedal-powered aircraft.
funFacts: On August 23, 1977, Bryan Allen pedalled the Gossamer Condor around the required figure-eight course to win the Kremer Prize.
The aircraft weighed about 32 kilograms, less than the pilot, and won designer Paul MacCready the £50,000 Kremer Prize.
Gliders climb by circling in thermals, columns of warm rising air that soaring birds have used for far longer than we have.

fun_strange_music_day.intro: Play something you would never normally play, or listen to a record that makes no sense to you. The rule for the day is simply that it must be unfamiliar.
funFacts: The day was started in 1998 by the New York musician Patrick Grant.
The theremin, built by Leon Theremin around 1920, is played by moving your hands near two antennas without ever touching it.
John Cage's prepared piano turns an ordinary grand into a percussion set by wedging screws and rubber between the strings.

fun_banana_split_day.intro: A banana lengthwise, three scoops, sauce, cream and a cherry on top. Absurdly over the top, which is exactly the point.
funFacts: The split is credited to David Strickler, a 23-year-old apprentice pharmacist in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, in 1904.
It cost ten cents at a time when a regular sundae went for five, and students from a nearby college spread the word.
The classic version pairs chocolate, vanilla and strawberry ice cream with chocolate, pineapple and strawberry sauces.

fun_dog_day.intro: For the friend who is delighted every single time you come home. A day for long walks, extra treats and far too many photographs.
funFacts: Dogs were the first animals humans domesticated, thousands of years before farming began.
A dog's nose print is as individual as a human fingerprint, and some registries use it as identification.
The area of a dog's brain devoted to smell is proportionally far larger than ours, which is why tracking work comes so easily.

fun_rock_paper_scissors_day.intro: The fairest decision-making tool ever invented, available anywhere, requiring nothing but two hands. Best of three, and no arguing afterwards.
funFacts: The game reached the West from Japan, where it is called janken; its ancestors are Chinese hand games described centuries earlier.
In 2005 a Japanese company chose between Christie's and Sotheby's for a major art sale by having them play rock paper scissors.
Because people rarely play randomly, tournament players study opponents' habits; beginners open with rock more often than chance would suggest.

fun_read_comics_in_public_day.intro: Take the comic out of the house, sit on a bench and read it where people can see. The whole idea is to stop treating panels and speech bubbles as a private pleasure.
funFacts: The day was launched in 2010 and set on 28 August, the birthday of the artist Jack Kirby.
Kirby co-created Captain America, the Fantastic Four and the X-Men, and drew tens of thousands of pages in his career.
A copy of Action Comics #1 from 1938, the first appearance of Superman, has sold for several million dollars.

fun_more_herbs_less_salt_day.intro: A cheerful nudge to reach for the basil, thyme and parsley before the salt cellar. Food gets more interesting, not less, when you swap one for the other.
funFacts: Basil, mint, rosemary, sage and thyme all belong to the same family, recognisable by their square stems.
Rosemary's botanical name comes from the Latin ros marinus, sea dew, after the coastal cliffs where it grows wild.
Dried herbs are more concentrated by volume than fresh ones, so recipes usually call for about a third as much.

fun_frankenstein_day.intro: A celebration of the novel that invented the mad scientist, the misunderstood creature and half of modern horror. It is held on its author's birthday.
funFacts: Mary Shelley was born on 30 August 1797 and had written Frankenstein by the age of nineteen.
The story began during the cold, rainy summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva, when the group challenged each other to write ghost stories.
Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature, which has no name at all in the book.

fun_trail_mix_day.intro: Nuts, raisins, seeds and, if nobody is looking, chocolate. The snack that fits in a jacket pocket and makes any walk feel like an expedition.
funFacts: German has had a word for it for centuries: Studentenfutter, student fodder, recorded since the 17th century.
English-speaking hikers often call it gorp, and argue endlessly about what the letters are supposed to stand for.
Nuts and dried fruit keep for months without cooling, which is why the mix travelled long before lightweight packaging existed.

fun_world_letter_writing_day.intro: A nudge to pick up a pen instead of a phone. A handwritten letter takes longer, costs a stamp and gets kept in a drawer for years, which is exactly the point.
funFacts: The day goes back to Australian artist Richard Simpkin, who spent years handwriting letters to people he admired.
Some of the oldest surviving letters are clay tablets from Mesopotamian traders, written roughly 4,000 years ago.
The Penny Black of 1840 was the first adhesive postage stamp and made sending a letter affordable for almost everyone.

fun_world_coconut_day.intro: A day for the palm that supplies food, drink, oil, rope and roofing all at once. In coconut-growing countries it is celebrated with markets, fairs and a lot of fresh coconut water.
funFacts: It has been marked on 2 September since 2009, the founding date of the community of coconut-producing countries.
Botanically a coconut is a drupe. Sharing this fruit type does not make it a close relative of plums or cherries.
Coconuts float and stay able to sprout after weeks at sea, which is how palms colonised tropical coastlines.

fun_skyscraper_day.intro: A day to crane your neck. Skyscrapers turned cities upward, and every generation has tried to build one taller than the last.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of architect Louis Sullivan, born on 3 September 1856 and known for the maxim 'form follows function'.
Chicago's ten-storey Home Insurance Building of 1885 is widely called the first skyscraper thanks to its steel frame.
The Burj Khalifa in Dubai has held the height record since 2010 at 828 metres.

fun_macadamia_nut_day.intro: A tribute to the buttery nut that grows on Australian rainforest trees. Rich, mild and famously hard to crack, which is why it usually arrives ready shelled.
funFacts: Macadamias are native to Australian rainforests and were named after the chemist John Macadam.
Their shells are among the toughest of any nut, so most macadamias are sold already cracked.
Hawaii became the centre of commercial growing after macadamia trees were planted there in the 1880s.

fun_be_late_for_something_day.intro: Official permission to stop rushing for once. The idea is not chronic tardiness but a few unhurried minutes: look around, finish the coffee, arrive slightly late and unbothered.
funFacts: The day was created by the Procrastinators' Club of America, founded in Philadelphia in 1956 by Les Waas.
Club founder Les Waas also wrote the jingle for the Mister Softee ice cream vans heard across the United States.
German universities still use the 'academic quarter': a lecture at nine actually starts at a quarter past.

fun_read_a_book_day.intro: A day with a very simple instruction: open a book and read it. No app, no notifications, just one story and however many pages you manage.
funFacts: Johannes Gutenberg's printing press of around 1450 turned books from rare treasures into everyday objects.
The Library of Congress is the world's largest library, holding well over 170 million items.
Iceland has the jolabokaflod, a Christmas book flood: books are given on 24 December and read the same night.

fun_salami_day.intro: A day for the sausage that keeps. Air-dried, spiced and sliced thin, salami was preserving meat centuries before anyone owned a fridge.
funFacts: The name comes from the Italian verb salare, to salt, the technique that made the sausage keep without cooling.
Salami develops its characteristic flavour through fermentation and drying. Some varieties use specially selected mould cultures on the casing.
Italy alone protects dozens of regional salami by law, from Milano to Felino and the small cacciatore sausages.

fun_star_trek_day.intro: The anniversary of the day the Enterprise first appeared on television. Fans celebrate with marathons, conventions and an unreasonable number of pointed ears.
funFacts: The first episode, 'The Man Trap', was broadcast on 8 September 1966.
After a fan write-in campaign, NASA named its first space shuttle Enterprise in 1976.
Mobile phone pioneer Martin Cooper named the series' flip communicator as an inspiration for his handset design.

fun_teddy_bear_day.intro: A day for the one toy almost everybody had. Teddy bears get hugged flat, lose an eye and still end up in a box in the attic rather than the bin.
funFacts: The name goes back to US President Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a tethered bear on a hunt in 1902.
Shopkeeper Morris Michtom put a stuffed bear in his New York window and asked Roosevelt for permission to call it a Teddy.
In Germany the Steiff company was making jointed toy bears at the same time, marked with the button in the ear from 1904.

fun_tv_dinner_day.intro: A nostalgic salute to dinner on a tray in front of the screen. The compartmented aluminium meal was 1950s convenience food and became a design icon by accident.
funFacts: Swanson launched the frozen tray meal in 1954 in a box printed to look like a television set.
