Company lore says a huge surplus of unsold Thanksgiving turkey gave someone the idea in the first place.
An original Swanson tray is part of the collection of the Smithsonian in Washington.

fun_hot_cross_bun_day.intro: A day for the spiced sweet bun with a cross on top. Traditionally British and traditionally Easter, but nobody has ever objected to eating one in September.
funFacts: Hot cross buns are enriched with spices and dried fruit, and the cross is usually piped on in flour paste.
A London decree of 1592 limited their sale to burials, Good Friday and Christmas, which made them a treat.
Folklore claimed a bun baked on Good Friday would never go mouldy, so sailors took them to sea for luck.

fun_blackberry_day.intro: A British day for the darkest fruit in the hedgerow, picked straight off the bramble in the middle of the season. Warm from the sun, purple fingers included.
funFacts: Despite the name a blackberry is not a berry at all: botanically it is an aggregate fruit made of many tiny drupelets.
British folklore says you should not pick blackberries after Old Michaelmas Day, 11 October, because the devil has spoiled them.
Mexico is the world's biggest producer of blackberries, with almost the whole crop grown for export.

fun_roald_dahl_day.intro: The birthday of the author behind Matilda, the BFG and the chocolate factory. Schools and libraries mark it with readings, costumes and a lot of invented vocabulary.
funFacts: Roald Dahl was born on 13 September 1916 in Llandaff in Wales to Norwegian parents.
He wrote in a small hut in his garden, on yellow paper, with six pencils sharpened before every session.
After his son's accident he helped develop the Wade-Dahl-Till valve, used to treat fluid on the brain.

fun_cream_filled_donut_day.intro: A day for the doughnut with no hole, because something better is hiding inside. Custard, whipped cream or jam, eaten in one go over a plate.
funFacts: By legend the hole in the ring doughnut was invented by American sailor Hanson Gregory in the 19th century.
The Boston cream doughnut has been the official state doughnut of Massachusetts since 2003.
Germany's Berliner and Austria's Krapfen are the same idea without the ring: filled, fried and dusted with sugar.

fun_linguine_day.intro: A day for the flat cousin of spaghetti. Slightly wider, slightly chewier and unbeatable with clams, seafood or a spoonful of green pesto.
funFacts: Linguine means 'little tongues' in Italian, a nod to the flattened cross section of the strands.
The shape comes from Liguria, the same coastal region that gave the world basil pesto.
Italy uses hundreds of pasta shapes, each matched to how well it carries a particular sauce.

fun_guacamole_day.intro: A day for the green dip that turns a bowl of tortilla chips into a meal. Avocado, lime, salt, and endless arguments about whether onion belongs in it.
funFacts: The word comes from the Nahuatl ahuacamolli, avocado sauce, and the dish was already eaten in Aztec Mexico.
Avocados only ripen after they are picked, so growers can use the tree itself as a natural storeroom.
Every Hass avocado descends from a single seedling grown by postman Rudolph Hass in California in the 1920s.

fun_apple_dumpling_day.intro: A whole apple, cored, filled with sugar and cinnamon and baked in a pastry coat. Autumn comfort food that fills the kitchen with the smell of the season.
funFacts: Apple dumplings are a Pennsylvania Dutch farmhouse classic and were once served for breakfast as often as dessert.
More than 7,500 apple cultivars are grown worldwide, but only a couple of dozen make it into supermarkets.
Apples float because roughly a quarter of their volume is air, which is what makes apple bobbing possible.

fun_world_bamboo_day.intro: A day for the plant that builds houses, scaffolding, floors, bicycles and dinner. Bamboo grows back faster than almost anything else you can build with.
funFacts: The day was declared in 2009 at the 8th World Bamboo Congress in Bangkok.
Bamboo is a grass, not a tree, and the fastest species can add up to 90 centimetres in a single day.
In Hong Kong, bamboo scaffolding is still tied together by hand around high-rise construction sites.

fun_talk_like_a_pirate_day.intro: One day a year when 'arrr' counts as a complete sentence. Offices, radio stations and schools join in, and nobody has to explain themselves.
funFacts: Two friends from Oregon, John Baur and Mark Summers, invented the day in 1995 while playing racquetball.
It went worldwide in 2002 after American columnist Dave Barry wrote about it in his newspaper column.
The classic pirate growl largely comes from actor Robert Newton's Long John Silver in the 1950 film Treasure Island.

fun_punch_day.intro: A day for the big shared bowl. Punch was the original party drink, ladled out for a whole room long before anyone shook a cocktail for one.
funFacts: The name is usually traced to the Hindi word for five, for the five parts: spirit, sugar, lemon, water and spice.
Sailors and traders of the East India Company brought the drink from India to Europe in the 17th century.
Georgian punch bowls could hold several litres and were passed around the table with a single large ladle.

fun_miniature_golf_day.intro: A day for windmills, loops and that one hole nobody ever manages in a single putt. Mini golf is golf with the walking, etiquette and expense removed.
funFacts: The Ladies' Putting Club at St Andrews, opened in 1867, is the oldest miniature golf course still in play.
Swiss architect Paul Bongni standardised the concrete course in 1954 and trademarked the name Minigolf.
It is a competitive sport with world championships, and players carry dozens of balls tuned for different obstacles.

fun_hobbit_day.intro: The shared birthday of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins. Fans celebrate by walking barefoot, eating far too much and reading a few chapters of Tolkien out loud.
funFacts: In the Shire Reckoning both Bilbo and Frodo were born on 22 September, which is where the date comes from.
The American Tolkien Society has promoted the day since 1978 as the centrepiece of Tolkien Week.
Hobbits are described as eating up to seven meals a day, second breakfast and elevenses included.

fun_checkers_day.intro: A dog gave this date its name: on 23 September 1952, Richard Nixon mentioned the family dog Checkers in a famous television address.
funFacts: The address became known as the “Checkers Speech”.
Checkers was a black-and-white cocker spaniel.
“Checkers” also names the board game known as draughts in Britain, but this date refers to the dog.

fun_world_gorilla_day.intro: A day for our huge, quiet, plant-eating relatives. Gorillas live in close family groups, and the imposing silverback is mostly a very patient babysitter.
funFacts: The day began in 2017, on the fiftieth anniversary of Dian Fossey's Karisoke Research Center in Rwanda.
Gorillas share roughly 98 percent of their DNA with humans, making them among our closest living relatives.
Every gorilla has a unique pattern of wrinkles above the nose, which researchers use like a fingerprint.

fun_comic_book_day.intro: A day for panels, speech bubbles and the shops that smell of paper. Superheroes, graphic novels and manga all count, and so does rereading the same issue again.
funFacts: Superman's debut in Action Comics No. 1 in 1938 launched the superhero genre; surviving copies now sell for millions.
In France and Belgium comics are called the ninth art, and Brussels has dozens of painted comic walls.
Japanese manga are read from right to left, and the weekly anthologies run to several hundred pages each.

fun_better_breakfast_day.intro: A day to take the first meal seriously for once. Not cereal standing at the counter, but a proper table, a warm drink and ten unhurried minutes.
funFacts: Breakfast literally means breaking the overnight fast, and the French dejeuner and Spanish desayuno say exactly the same thing.
Cornflakes came out of the Kellogg brothers' sanatorium kitchen in the 1890s, from a batch of wheat left standing too long.
Breakfast looks wildly different around the world: rice congee in China, ful medames in Egypt, fresh rolls in Germany.

fun_world_tourism_day.intro: A day for the pleasure of going somewhere else. Packing a bag, getting lost in an unfamiliar street and coming home with stories is one of life's cheapest luxuries.
funFacts: The day has been held since 1980 and marks the adoption of the world tourism organisation's statutes in 1970.
France has been the world's most visited country for decades, ahead of Spain and the United States.
The word tourist appeared in English around 1800, when the Grand Tour was the finishing school of the wealthy.

fun_good_neighbor_day.intro: A day for the people who take in your parcels and water your plants. Neighbourliness is small, unglamorous and the reason a street feels like somewhere to live.
funFacts: The idea came from Becky Mattson of Lakeside, Montana, in the early 1970s; President Carter proclaimed the day in 1978.
The English word neighbour comes from Old English roots meaning roughly 'the near dweller'.
Fred Rogers opened his children's programme with 'Won't You Be My Neighbor?' for more than thirty years.

fun_biscotti_day.intro: A day for the hard almond biscuit that is meant to be dunked. Coffee, tea or sweet wine, biscotti soften just enough and never fall apart in the cup.
funFacts: Biscotti means twice baked: the dough is baked as a loaf, sliced, then baked again until dry.
That dryness made them travel food, and hard twice-baked biscuits fed Roman soldiers and later sailors for months.
In Tuscany the almond version is called cantuccio and is traditionally dipped in sweet Vin Santo.

fun_mulled_cider_day.intro: A day for the mug that warms your hands. Apple juice or cider heated with cinnamon, cloves and orange, and suddenly the end of September feels cosy rather than grey.
funFacts: In North America cider means cloudy unfiltered apple juice, while in Britain it is the alcoholic drink.
Mulling means gently heating a drink with spices, the same method behind mulled wine.
It takes roughly three dozen apples to press a single gallon of cider, which is about four litres.

fun_international_coffee_day.intro: A worldwide toast to the bean that gets most of the planet out of bed. Filter, espresso or cold brew – the point is to enjoy the cup and spare a thought for the people who grow it.
funFacts: The International Coffee Organization launched the shared date in Milan in 2015; several countries had been holding their own coffee day before that.
Finland drinks more coffee per head than any other country, well over ten kilograms of roasted beans per person a year.
A coffee cherry normally holds two flat-sided seeds; when only one round seed forms, it is called a peaberry.

fun_name_your_car_day.intro: Plenty of people talk to their car anyway, so today it officially gets a name. A silly little ritual that turns a lump of metal into a member of the household.
funFacts: Cars have collected nicknames since the beginning: Ford's Model T was known to everyone as the Tin Lizzie.
Herbie, the Volkswagen Beetle of the Disney films, races with the number 53, borrowed from baseball pitcher Don Drysdale.
The Beetle itself is named after insects around the world: Käfer in Germany, coccinelle (ladybird) in France, maggiolino (may bug) in Italy.

fun_mean_girls_day.intro: One line of film dialogue turned 3 October into a fan holiday. Every year the internet quotes it, wears pink and rewatches the whole comedy.
funFacts: The date comes from a single scene: Aaron turns around, asks Cady what day it is, and she answers that it is October 3rd.
Tina Fey wrote the screenplay after reading Rosalind Wiseman's non-fiction book about teenage cliques, Queen Bees and Wannabes.
Fans often wear pink on the day, a nod to the film's rule that the clique dresses in pink on Wednesdays.

fun_taco_day.intro: A folded tortilla, a filling, a squeeze of lime – and an endless argument about the right one. Today every version counts, from street-stall al pastor to the crunchy shell at home.
funFacts: In 19th-century Mexican silver mines a taco was a paper-wrapped charge of gunpowder, which is the likeliest source of the food's name.
Tacos al pastor grew out of the spit-roasted meat that Lebanese immigrants brought to Mexico in the early 20th century.
The pre-formed crunchy shell is a US invention that spread with fast-food chains from the 1950s onwards.

fun_james_bond_day.intro: Shaken, not stirred: the day marks the anniversary of the very first Bond film and belongs to everyone who enjoys gadgets, chase scenes and a good title song.
funFacts: The first Global James Bond Day was held on 5 October 2012, fifty years to the day after Dr. No premiered in London.
Ian Fleming borrowed the name from the American ornithologist James Bond, author of the field guide Birds of the West Indies.
Six actors have played 007 in the official film series so far, from Sean Connery to Daniel Craig.

fun_mad_hatter_day.intro: A day for cheerful nonsense, borrowed from Lewis Carroll's tea party. The invitation is simple: be a little more absurd than usual and put the kettle on.
funFacts: The date comes from the card in the Hatter's hatband in John Tenniel's 1865 illustrations: 10/6, a price of ten shillings and sixpence.
Computer staff in Boulder, Colorado declared the day in 1986 as an antidote to overly serious workdays.
The saying mad as a hatter is older than the book: hat makers worked with mercury compounds, which damaged the nervous system.

fun_frappe_day.intro: Instant coffee, sugar and water shaken into a thick foam, then poured over ice: the frappe is Greece's gift to hot afternoons, and it was invented completely by accident.
funFacts: The drink was improvised at the 1957 Thessaloniki trade fair, when a Nestle representative had no hot water for his coffee.
In Greece you order it sketos, metrios or glykos, meaning without sugar, with some, or sweet.
The foam only works with instant coffee: its soluble powder whips up in a way that freshly brewed coffee cannot.

fun_world_octopus_day.intro: A day for the most alien-looking clever animal in the ocean. Eight arms, an escape-artist reputation and a talent for opening jars make the octopus hard not to admire.
funFacts: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, because it carries oxygen with copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron.
About two thirds of its neurons sit in the arms, which can feel and taste on their own.
It changes colour and texture within a fraction of a second, even though its eyes are almost certainly colour-blind.

fun_beer_and_pizza_day.intro: The most reliable pairing in the world gets its own date. A hot slice, a cold glass, no cutlery required – ideally shared with other people.
funFacts: Legend has it the Margherita's basil, mozzarella and tomato were chosen for Queen Margherita's visit to Naples in 1889.
The craft of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage since 2017.
The Bavarian purity law of 1516 named only barley, hops and water; yeast was still unknown as an ingredient.

fun_cake_decorating_day.intro: Today the icing matters more than the sponge. Piping bag, spatula and a steady hand turn an ordinary cake into something people photograph before they eat it.
funFacts: The piping bag is usually credited to the French chef Antonin Careme, who built showpiece confections in the early 19th century.
Royal icing, the hard white kind, is said to owe its name to Queen Victoria's wedding cake of 1840.
Rolled fondant is laid over a cake in one sheet, which is why the surface can look as smooth as porcelain.

fun_dulce_de_leche_day.intro: Milk and sugar, stirred until they turn deep brown and spreadable. South America's favourite sweet goes on toast, into pastries and, most often, straight onto a spoon.
funFacts: The Argentinian dulce de leche trade association has promoted 11 October as its day since 1998.
The colour and flavour come from slow caramelisation and browning reactions between milk sugar and milk protein.
A popular legend puts its invention in 1829, when a maid supposedly forgot a pot of sweetened milk on the stove.

fun_gumbo_day.intro: Louisiana in a bowl: a thick stew of roux, stock and whatever the region offers, served over rice. Every family cooks it slightly differently and defends its version.
funFacts: Everything starts with the roux, flour cooked in fat and stirred until it goes from blond to dark chocolate brown.
The name most likely comes from a West African word for okra, one of the classic thickeners.
Louisiana declared gumbo its official state cuisine in 2004.

fun_treat_yo_self_day.intro: A sitcom invented it and fans kept it: one day a year for guilt-free indulgence, whether that means new shoes, a long bath or an absurdly large dessert.
funFacts: The phrase comes from the Parks and Recreation episode Pawnee Rangers, first broadcast on 13 October 2011.
In the show Tom and Donna spend the day on clothes, fragrances, massages, mimosas and fine leather goods.
Their friend Ben joins in and blows his budget on a full Batman costume, which he then refuses to take off.

fun_dessert_day.intro: The course everyone claims to have no room for and then finishes anyway. Cake, pudding, ice cream or fruit – today the sweet ending is the main event.
funFacts: The word dessert comes from the French desservir, to clear the table: it was what arrived after everything else was taken away.
Tiramisu is surprisingly young; the recipe is traced to restaurants around Treviso in the 1960s and 70s.
A baked Alaska survives the oven because whipped egg white is full of air and insulates the ice cream underneath.

fun_pug_day.intro: Snorting, wrinkled and thoroughly convinced of its own charm: the pug gets a day of its own. A breed built entirely for company rather than work.
funFacts: Pugs come from China, where they were bred centuries ago as lapdogs for the imperial court.
A group of pugs is traditionally called a grumble.
In the Netherlands the pug became a symbol of the House of Orange after one is said to have woken William the Silent in time.

fun_world_bread_day.intro: Flour, water, salt and time. Bread is the most ordinary food there is and one of the most varied – today bakers and home bakers celebrate exactly that.
funFacts: Bakers' associations started the day in 2006, deliberately placing it alongside World Food Day on 16 October.
German bread culture, with more than 3,000 registered varieties, is listed as national intangible cultural heritage.
Sourdough rises without added yeast: wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria in the starter do the work.

fun_mulligan_day.intro: In golf a mulligan is a shot you simply take again, unpunished. The day borrows that idea for everything else: one friendly do-over, no questions asked.
funFacts: The most repeated origin story credits the Canadian golfer David Mulligan, who re-teed a bad drive in Montreal in the 1920s.
The official rules of golf do not recognise the mulligan at all; it exists only in friendly rounds.
Charity tournaments often sell mulligans in advance, which turns a bad shot into a donation.

fun_necktie_day.intro: Croatia celebrates the accessory it gave the world. The cravat travelled from a soldier's neck cloth to the boardroom – and the knot is still a small daily ritual.
funFacts: The word cravat goes back to Croatian soldiers in 17th-century France, whose knotted neck cloths became a court fashion.
In 2003 a huge red cravat was tied around the Roman amphitheatre in Pula to mark the day.
The modern tie owes its shape to Jesse Langsdorf, who patented cutting the fabric on the bias in 1924.

fun_gin_and_tonic_day.intro: Two ingredients, endless variations: gin, tonic, ice and something citrus. A drink that started out as medicine and became the easiest cocktail in the world.
funFacts: British troops in India mixed bitter quinine tonic with gin, sugar and lime to make their malaria prophylaxis drinkable.
The quinine in tonic water fluoresces under ultraviolet light, which makes the glass glow pale blue.
London Dry Gin is a production method, not a place of origin: it can legally be distilled anywhere in the world.

fun_sloth_day.intro: The slowest mammal in the tree tops gets its own day. Sloths do everything at half speed and still manage to be excellent swimmers – a good argument for taking your time.
funFacts: The Colombian wildlife foundation AIUNAU started the day in 2010 after an international sloth meeting in Medellin.
Sloth fur grows from the belly towards the back, so rain runs off while the animal hangs upside down.
Green algae grow in that fur as camouflage, and specialised sloth moths live in it too.

fun_apple_day.intro: A British autumn celebration of apples and the orchards they come from, with tastings, pressing and forgotten varieties on the table.
funFacts: The charity Common Ground held the first Apple Day on 21 October 1990 in London's Covent Garden.
The National Fruit Collection in Kent keeps more than 2,000 apple varieties growing side by side.
Apple pips never grow true to the parent tree, so every orchard variety is propagated by grafting.

fun_wombat_day.intro: Australia's sturdy burrowing marsupial gets a day of appreciation. Short legs, powerful claws and an unbothered attitude have earned the wombat a lot of fans.
funFacts: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings, which stay put on rocks instead of rolling away.
Their pouch opens backwards, so digging does not fill it with soil while a joey is inside.
The rear end is reinforced with tough cartilage, and wombats use it to block the entrance of their burrow.

fun_mole_day.intro: Chemistry's own party: from 6:02 in the morning to 6:02 in the evening on 10/23, classrooms celebrate the unit that makes counting atoms possible.
funFacts: The date and time spell out Avogadro's number, 6.02 times ten to the twenty-third.
Since the 2019 redefinition of the SI units, one mole contains exactly 6.02214076 times ten to the twenty-third particles.
The idea appeared in a chemistry teachers' journal in the 1980s; the National Mole Day Foundation followed in 1991.

fun_bologna_day.intro: The pale pink slice between two pieces of bread: bologna is unglamorous lunchbox food with an Italian ancestor and a lot of nostalgia attached.
funFacts: The sausage takes its name from Bologna's mortadella, but leaves out the cubes of fat and the pistachios.
Mortadella di Bologna has carried EU protected geographical indication status since 1998.
In the United States a 1970s advertising jingle that spelled out the name made bologna a household word.

fun_world_pasta_day.intro: Durum wheat, water, boiling salted water: pasta is the cheapest reliable happiness there is. The day was invented by pasta makers and adopted by everyone else.
funFacts: The date was proclaimed at the first World Pasta Congress in Rome on 25 October 1995.
Italy counts hundreds of shapes, and the same shape often carries a different name from region to region.
Italian law requires dried pasta to be made from durum wheat semolina, which is what keeps it firm when cooked.

fun_pumpkin_day.intro: Soup, pie, lantern or doorstep decoration: October belongs to the pumpkin. Today it is celebrated as a vegetable rather than a face with a candle in it.
funFacts: Botanically a pumpkin is a berry, and it belongs to the same family as cucumbers and melons.
Competition growers have pushed the world record for a single pumpkin past 1,200 kilograms.
Before pumpkins were available, Irish lanterns were carved from turnips and beets.

fun_black_cat_day.intro: A day for the cats that get overlooked. Black cats wait longest in shelters and photograph badly – and are otherwise exactly like every other cat.
funFacts: The British charity Cats Protection started the day in 2011 because black cats were being adopted more slowly than others.
In Britain and Japan a black cat crossing your path is considered lucky, while much of continental Europe reads it the other way round.
Most black cats carry a hidden tabby pattern that becomes visible in bright sunlight.

fun_international_animation_day.intro: Drawn, modelled or rendered: today celebrates the art of making still images move, and the enormous patience it takes to do it well.
funFacts: The date marks 28 October 1892, when Emile Reynaud showed his Theatre Optique to a paying audience in Paris.
The international animation association ASIFA has organised screenings on the day since 2002.
Film normally runs at 24 frames a second; hand-drawn animation often uses one drawing for two or three frames.

fun_internet_day.intro: The day the network first spoke. It celebrates the very first message sent between two distant computers – which promptly crashed halfway through.
funFacts: On 29 October 1969 UCLA sent the word login to Stanford; the system failed after the letters L and O.
The ARPANET started with four nodes: UCLA, the Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara and the University of Utah.
The smiley made of a colon and a bracket was proposed by computer scientist Scott Fahlman in 1982.

fun_candy_corn_day.intro: Three stripes of sugar in the shape of a kernel of corn: America's most divisive sweet. People either eat a whole bag or refuse to touch it.
funFacts: Candy corn was created in the 1880s by George Renninger at the Wunderlee Candy Company in Philadelphia.
It was originally marketed to farmers as chicken feed and sold all year, not just in autumn.
The white, orange and yellow layers were once poured into moulds by hand, one colour after another.

fun_magic_day.intro: Cards, coins and a little misdirection: magicians mark this date in memory of Harry Houdini, who died on 31 October 1926.
funFacts: Houdini led the Society of American Magicians for nine years, and the society has kept the date ever since.
His best known escapes involved handcuffs, straitjackets and the water-filled Chinese Water Torture Cell.
The cups and balls routine is one of the oldest recorded tricks; Hieronymus Bosch painted a version around 1500.

fun_world_vegan_day.intro: A day for plant-based cooking and for everyone curious about it. Markets, cafés and kitchens show off what happens when meat, milk and eggs simply stay out of the recipe.
funFacts: Donald Watson coined the word vegan in 1944 by taking the first three and last two letters of vegetarian.
The date marks the fiftieth birthday of the UK Vegan Society, celebrated for the first time in November 1994.
Aquafaba, the liquid from a tin of chickpeas, whips up like egg white and turns into meringue.

fun_deviled_egg_day.intro: Halved boiled eggs, the yolk mashed with mustard, mayonnaise and a dusting of paprika, then piped back in. A buffet classic that disappears faster than anything else on the table.
funFacts: Stuffed eggs were already served in ancient Rome, seasoned with spicy sauces at the start of a banquet.
In English cooking, deviled has meant highly spiced since the 18th century, long before the eggs got the name.
In parts of the American South they are politely called stuffed or dressed eggs to avoid the word devil.

fun_sandwich_day.intro: The birthday of the man who lent his name to the world's most practical meal: two slices of bread and whatever you like in between. Portable, endlessly variable and never out of fashion.
funFacts: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, was born on 3 November 1718; the food was named after him, not the other way round.
The earl took his title from the town of Sandwich in Kent, on the English Channel coast.
The word first appears as a food in a 1762 journal entry by the historian Edward Gibbon.

fun_king_tut_day.intro: On this date in 1922 a shovel struck a stone step in the Valley of the Kings. It led to the only pharaoh's tomb ever found almost untouched, and to a worldwide Egypt craze.
funFacts: Howard Carter's team uncovered the first step on 4 November 1922; the antechamber was opened three weeks later.
Asked whether he could see anything, Carter is said to have answered: Yes, wonderful things.
The tomb held more than 5,000 objects, among them a gold death mask weighing roughly ten kilograms.

fun_guy_fawkes_night.intro: Britain's bonfire night: fireworks over the rooftops, sparklers in cold hands and something sticky and sweet to eat. The whole country remembers a plot that famously never came off.
funFacts: The rhyme still learned by heart begins: Remember, remember the fifth of November.
Traditional food includes toffee apples, bonfire toffee and parkin, a sticky ginger cake from northern England.
Lewes in Sussex holds the largest celebrations, with several societies parading through town by torchlight.

fun_saxophone_day.intro: A birthday party for the instrument that gave jazz its voice. Adolphe Sax wanted something that carried like a brass instrument but sang like a woodwind, and he got both.
funFacts: Adolphe Sax was born on 6 November 1814 in Dinant, Belgium, and patented the saxophone in 1846.
Although it is made of brass, the saxophone counts as a woodwind because its sound starts at a single reed.
Sax survived a startling run of childhood accidents, including a fall from a height and swallowing a needle.

fun_bittersweet_chocolate_with_almonds_d.intro: Dark chocolate, whole almonds, nothing else needed. The bitter cocoa and the buttery crunch are one of those pairings nobody had to invent twice.
funFacts: In the United States a bar may only be sold as bittersweet if it contains at least 35 percent cacao.
Almonds are not nuts: botanically they are the seed inside a stone fruit, making them close relatives of the peach.
The Aztecs used cacao beans as money; a few beans were enough to buy a meal at market.

fun_cook_something_bold_day.intro: Permission to reach for the garlic, the chilli and the ripest cheese in the fridge. The idea is a kitchen smell so bold that the whole building knows what is for dinner.
funFacts: The day was thought up by Thomas and Ruth Roy, a couple from Pennsylvania who have registered dozens of odd observances.
Garlic only smells of garlic once it is cut: crushing the cells releases allicin, which is absent in the whole clove.
Durian smells so strongly that it is banned from buses and trains in Singapore, complete with a warning pictogram.

fun_inventors_day.intro: Germany, Austria and Switzerland celebrate inventors on the birthday of Hedy Lamarr, a film star who also co-invented a radio technique still at work in your pocket today.
funFacts: Hedy Lamarr was born in Vienna on 9 November 1914 and became a Hollywood star in the 1930s.
With composer George Antheil she patented frequency hopping in 1942, an idea later echoed in wireless technology.
The German-language Inventors' Day was launched in 2005 by the Austrian inventor Gerhard Muthenthaler.

fun_area_code_day.intro: The day the telephone learned to find its own way. On this date in 1951 a customer dialled clear across the United States for the first time without asking an operator for help.
funFacts: On 10 November 1951 Englewood's mayor M. Leslie Denning rang his counterpart Frank Osborne in Alameda, California, himself, with no operator in between.
It took three digits of area code plus a seven-digit number, and that ten-digit pattern still holds across North America.
AT&T's first nationwide numbering plan of October 1947 carved North America into 86 area codes, with room for 152.

fun_origami_day.intro: A square of paper, no scissors, no glue. Japan marks the day with folded cranes, and the same craft turns up in engineering whenever something large has to become small.
funFacts: A senbazuru is a garland of a thousand folded cranes, traditionally given as a wish for health or peace.
Akira Yoshizawa developed the folding notation used worldwide and is said to have created some 50,000 models.
The Miura fold, an origami pattern, has been used to pack solar panels for spacecraft so they open in one pull.

fun_pizza_with_the_works_day.intro: Order everything the kitchen has, then draw one firm line. The longest, most opinionated name on the food-day calendar, and a reliable way to start an argument at the table.
funFacts: The works means every topping on the menu at once, a phrase American diners have used for generations.
Anchovies land at the bottom of almost every survey of favourite pizza toppings in the United States.
The Margherita of 1889 was built the other way round: tomato, mozzarella and basil, and nothing more.

fun_world_kindness_day.intro: A day with one very simple task: do something friendly that nobody asked for. A message, a seat offered, a coffee paid forward — small gestures, deliberately made visible for once.
funFacts: The World Kindness Movement was founded at a Tokyo conference in 1997; the day has been marked since 1998.
In Naples the caffè sospeso is over a century old: you pay for two coffees and leave one for a stranger.
Singapore has had a kindness mascot since 1982, a friendly lion called Singa who campaigns for everyday courtesy.

fun_pickle_day.intro: Sour, crunchy and impossible to eat quietly. A day for the cucumber that spent a few weeks in brine and came out with far more personality than it went in with.
funFacts: Cucumbers turn into pickles two ways: lactic acid fermentation in salt brine, or a quick bath in hot vinegar.
The Spreewald gherkin from Brandenburg has carried a protected EU geographical indication since 1999.
In the United States the brine is bottled and sold as a sports drink, popular against muscle cramps.

fun_spicy_hermit_cookie_day.intro: A soft, dark, heavily spiced bar cookie from New England: molasses, cinnamon, cloves and raisins. Built to keep, which is exactly why sailors loved them.
funFacts: Hermits get their colour and chew from molasses, and their warmth from cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and ginger.
They keep for weeks and improve after a day or two, so New England crews took them on long voyages.
Recipes turn up in American cookbooks from the late 19th century; where the name comes from is still disputed.

fun_button_day.intro: In praise of the small disc that holds everything together. Collectors sort them by material, age and pattern, and anyone who has ever opened a button tin knows how quickly time passes.
funFacts: The day goes back to the National Button Society, founded in 1938, which made collecting a recognised hobby.
Buttons are around 5,000 years old, but they were ornaments first: the buttonhole only appeared in medieval Europe.
Men's shirts button left over right and women's the other way round; every explanation for it is a theory.

fun_take_a_hike_day.intro: Boots on, phone in the pocket, out of the door. November light, cold air and a marked trail are all it takes — the good part is that any distance counts.
funFacts: The Appalachian Trail runs about 3,500 kilometres; walking it in one go takes most people five to seven months.
The European long-distance path E1 leads roughly 8,000 kilometres from northern Norway down to Sicily.
Germany alone is criss-crossed by around 200,000 kilometres of waymarked hiking trails.

fun_apple_cider_day.intro: Freshly pressed, cloudy and unfiltered, usually served warm with a stick of cinnamon. In North America cider is the drink that makes autumn taste like autumn.
funFacts: In the United States cider means unfermented cloudy apple juice; the alcoholic version is called hard cider.
It takes roughly a kilogram and a half of apples to press a single litre of juice.
More than 7,500 apple varieties are grown worldwide, and blending several of them is what gives cider its depth.

fun_carbonated_beverage_with_caffeine_da.intro: A day with a wonderfully bureaucratic name for something very ordinary: the cold, fizzy, faintly buzzing drink in the tall glass with ice.
funFacts: Joseph Priestley worked out how to dissolve carbon dioxide in water in 1767, above a brewery vat in Leeds.
A 330 millilitre glass of cola holds around 35 milligrams of caffeine, roughly a third of a cup of filter coffee.
The tingle of fizzy drinks is not the bubbles but carbonic acid, picked up by the same receptors as sour taste.

fun_absurdity_day.intro: A day set aside for the gloriously pointless. Nonsense, contradictions and ideas that fall apart the moment you think about them — and are all the more enjoyable for it.
funFacts: The critic Martin Esslin coined the term Theatre of the Absurd in 1960 for plays by Beckett, Ionesco and others.
The Ig Nobel Prizes have honoured research since 1991 that first makes you laugh and then makes you think.
Monty Python's Ministry of Silly Walks sketch, first shown in 1970, is still the most-quoted piece of nonsense.

fun_world_hello_day.intro: The task is charmingly small: greet ten people. The idea behind it is that talking to each other, however briefly, is still the cheapest way to avoid a conflict.
funFacts: Brothers Brian and Michael McCormack started the day in 1973, in response to a war in the Middle East.
People in well over 100 countries now take part, and several Nobel Peace Prize laureates have endorsed it.
Hello owes its career to the telephone: Edison pushed for it, while Alexander Graham Bell preferred Ahoy.

fun_kimchi_day.intro: South Korea's fermented cabbage has its own official date. Sharp, salty, alive with lactic acid — and in Korea a side dish so familiar it feels like a member of the household.
funFacts: South Korea made 22 November an official day in 2020: eleven ingredients that unfold twenty-two benefits.
Kimjang, making kimchi together as neighbours and family, joined the UNESCO intangible heritage list in 2013.
Korean kitchens often have a dedicated kimchi fridge, which holds a steady low temperature for the fermentation.

fun_fibonacci_day.intro: Write the date as 11/23 and you have 1, 1, 2, 3 — the opening of the most famous number sequence there is. Every term is simply the sum of the two before it.
funFacts: Leonardo of Pisa introduced the sequence to Europe in 1202 in Liber Abaci, using a puzzle about breeding rabbits.
Divide any term by the one before it and you close in on the golden ratio, roughly 1.618.
Count the spirals in a sunflower head or on a pine cone and you usually land on two neighbouring Fibonacci numbers.

fun_evolution_day.intro: On this date in 1859 a book appeared that rearranged the way we see living things. Darwin had been sitting on his idea for twenty years before he finally let it out.
funFacts: On the Origin of Species went on sale on 24 November 1859; the entire first print run was spoken for that same day.
Darwin avoided the noun evolution almost entirely — the first edition simply ends on the word evolved.
The voyage of the Beagle that supplied his material lasted nearly five years, from 1831 to 1836.

fun_parfait_day.intro: Layer upon layer in a tall glass, and the glass is half the point. Fruit, cream, something crunchy — the French original was frozen, the modern one usually is not.
funFacts: Parfait simply means perfect; the French version is a frozen cream dessert made with sugar syrup and egg yolk.
The American parfait is layered instead: yoghurt or ice cream with fruit and granola, served cold in a tall glass.
Parfait glasses are deliberately narrow and high so that every single layer stays visible from the outside.

fun_cake_day.intro: No occasion needed today: cake is the occasion. Whether it is a plain sponge or four floors of buttercream, the day exists purely so that a slice can be cut.
funFacts: The English word cake comes from the Old Norse kaka and originally meant a small flat baked good.
Candles on a birthday cake are usually traced back to the German Kinderfeste of the 18th century.
Cakes only became reliably light after 1843, when Alfred Bird developed a workable baking powder in Birmingham.

fun_electric_guitar_day.intro: Held on Jimi Hendrix's birthday, in honour of six strings, a pickup and an amplifier. No instrument changed the sound of the last century quite so thoroughly.
funFacts: Jimi Hendrix was born on 27 November 1942 in Seattle; left-handed, he simply restrung a right-handed guitar.
The first commercially successful electric guitar, the 1932 Frying Pan lap steel, was named after a kitchen pan.
Fender launched the Broadcaster in 1950; the name Telecaster followed in 1951.

fun_red_planet_day.intro: The date honours the launch of Mariner 4 in 1964, the probe that sent back humanity's first close-up pictures of Mars. Ever since, the fourth planet has felt like a neighbour.
funFacts: Mariner 4 launched on 28 November 1964 and returned 21 complete images and part of a 22nd during its Mars flyby in July 1965.
Mars looks red because its dust is full of iron oxide — the planet is, quite literally, rusty.
Olympus Mons rises about 22 kilometres above the plains around it, the tallest volcano in the solar system.

fun_square_dance_day.intro: Four couples, one square and a caller shouting out the next move. Nobody has to know the choreography in advance, which is exactly what makes it so easy to join in.
funFacts: The dance grew out of English country dances, the French quadrille and Irish and Scottish figures.
A caller announces every figure live, so dancers follow instructions rather than a memorised routine.
Modern square dance calls are given in English worldwide, so a dancer from Japan can join a set in Sweden.

fun_mason_jar_day.intro: A glass jar with a screw thread and a sealing lid — an everyday object so well designed that it has barely changed in over 160 years. Today it holds salad, drinks and fairy lights.
funFacts: John Landis Mason patented his screw-neck preserving jar on 30 November 1858.
Patented Nov 30th 1858 was still being moulded into jars decades later, long after the patent had run out.
Mason sold his rights early and earned little from the invention; he died in poverty in New York in 1902.

fun_eat_a_red_apple_day.intro: A cheerful nudge to open December with something crisp: pick a red apple, polish it on your sleeve and enjoy the crunch. About as low-effort as a celebration can get.
funFacts: Botanists trace the cultivated apple back to wild trees in the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, where apple forests still grow.
Roughly a quarter of an apple's volume is air, which is why apples bob happily in a tub of water.
More than 7,500 apple cultivars exist worldwide, from tiny crab apples to varieties bred purely for cider.

fun_mutt_day.intro: A day for mixed-breed dogs, the one-off characters whose ancestry is anybody's guess. It celebrates dogs that look like no other and nudges people towards the shelter.
funFacts: Mixed-breed dogs often benefit from hybrid vigour, the genetic advantage of drawing on a wider gene pool.
Laika, the first dog to orbit the Earth, was a mixed-breed stray picked up on the streets of Moscow.
The word mutt is short for muttonhead, an American insult from around 1900 that later softened into affection.

fun_make_a_gift_day.intro: Three weeks before Christmas, this day suggests making a present instead of buying one. Baked, knitted, drawn or built: the point is that somebody spent time rather than money.
funFacts: Modern gift wrap was an accident: in 1917 the Hall brothers ran out of tissue and sold decorative envelope liners instead.
A Japanese furoshiki cloth wraps the gift and is reused afterwards, so the wrapping is part of the present.
Ribbon curls because the scissor blade stretches one side of the plastic more than the other, forcing it into a spiral.

fun_cookie_day.intro: A whole day for the cookie in every form: crisp, chewy, iced or dunked in milk. December is the obvious slot, right in the middle of baking season.
funFacts: The day was launched in 1987 by the American bakery chain Blue Chip Cookies.
The word cookie comes from the Dutch koekje, little cake, and reached English through the Dutch settlers of New York.
In 2019 astronauts baked cookies aboard the International Space Station in an oven built for zero gravity.

fun_day_of_the_ninja.intro: An internet-born celebration of the ninja: black outfit, silent footsteps, throwing stars. Fans mark it by dressing up, watching ninja films and moving suspiciously quietly.
funFacts: Historical shinobi came mainly from the Iga and Kōga regions of Japan and worked as scouts, spies and saboteurs.
The all-black outfit comes from kabuki theatre, where audiences agreed to treat stagehands dressed in black as invisible.
Iga in Mie Prefecture runs a ninja museum with revolving walls and trapdoors, plus an annual ninja festival.

fun_microwave_oven_day.intro: A salute to the humble box that turns leftovers into dinner in ninety seconds. Few kitchen appliances are mocked so often and used so relentlessly.
funFacts: Percy Spencer noticed in 1945 that a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he stood beside an active radar magnetron.
The first commercial Radarange of 1947 stood nearly 1.8 metres tall, weighed around 340 kilograms and was water-cooled.
Household microwaves run at 2.45 gigahertz, a frequency that sets the water molecules in food spinning and warms it.

fun_cotton_candy_day.intro: Spun sugar on a stick, mostly air and gone in seconds. The day honours a fairground classic that turns a spoonful of sugar into a cloud the size of a head.
funFacts: The spinning machine was patented in 1899 by the dentist William Morrison together with confectioner John C. Wharton.
Sold as Fairy Floss at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, it shifted more than 68,000 boxes at 25 cents each.
Germans call it Zuckerwatte, sugar wool, while the French order barbe à papa, meaning dad's beard.

fun_brownie_day.intro: Dense, fudgy and stuck somewhere between cake and biscuit: the brownie gets its own December date. Whether the corner piece or the middle one wins remains unsettled.
funFacts: The brownie is credited to Chicago's Palmer House Hotel, which served a chocolate bar cake at the 1893 World's Fair.
The Brownies in the 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book were made with molasses and contained no chocolate at all.
The Palmer House still bakes its version to the old recipe, finished with a glossy apricot glaze.

fun_christmas_card_day.intro: A nod to the first commercial Christmas card, printed in London in 1843. A good excuse to write a few lines by hand while everyone else is sending messages.
funFacts: Henry Cole commissioned the card because he had no time to answer his letters one by one; John Callcott Horsley drew it.
Around 1,000 copies were lithographed, coloured by hand and sold for a shilling each.
The design drew complaints because it showed a child being handed a glass of wine at the family table.

fun_dewey_decimal_system_day.intro: The birthday of Melvil Dewey, born on 10 December 1851, whose numbering scheme still tells you where a book sits on the shelf. A quiet celebration of order among the stacks.
funFacts: Dewey published his classification anonymously in 1876 while working in the library of Amherst College.
The system splits all knowledge into ten main classes and then into tens again, so 796 lands you at sport.
Libraries in more than 130 countries use it, and it has been translated into over 30 languages.

fun_tango_day.intro: Argentina celebrates the tango on the birthday of its most famous singer. Bandoneón, close embrace and a dance that turned a port-city sound into a world language.
funFacts: The date marks the birthday of singer Carlos Gardel in 1890 and of violinist Julio De Caro in 1899.
UNESCO added tango to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2009, jointly for Argentina and Uruguay.
The bandoneón was built in Germany for chapel music long before it became the defining sound of Buenos Aires.

fun_gingerbread_house_day.intro: A day for edible architecture: walls of spiced dough, icing as mortar and sweets on the roof. Structural failure is part of the fun.
funFacts: The custom took off in Germany after the Brothers Grimm published Hansel and Gretel with its witch's house in 1812.
Nuremberg's Lebkuchen bakers had their own guild, and the city's spiced cakes were traded right across Europe.
The largest gingerbread house on record, built in Texas in 2013, used around 3,000 kilograms of flour and 7,200 eggs.

fun_violin_day.intro: Four strings, a wooden box and a bow strung with horsehair. From concert halls to village fiddling, no instrument moves between worlds quite so easily.
funFacts: The violin took its familiar shape in 16th-century Cremona, where Andrea Amati built instruments that still survive.
A violin is assembled from around 70 separate pieces of wood, usually spruce for the top and maple for the back.
Antonio Stradivari is thought to have made about 1,100 instruments, of which roughly 650 still exist.

fun_monkey_day.intro: A day for monkeys and, loosely, all primates. It began as an art-school joke and grew into a fixture for zoos, illustrators and wildlife groups.
funFacts: Monkey Day was started in 2000 by the American art students Casey Sorrow and Eric Millikin.
Monkeys and apes differ mainly by the tail: monkeys usually have one, gorillas, chimpanzees and gibbons do not.
Japanese macaques in Jigokudani bathe in hot springs through the winter, a habit first observed in the 1960s.

fun_cupcake_day.intro: One cake, one person, no knife required. The cupcake gets its December date, complete with swirled frosting and a fluted paper case.
funFacts: Amelia Simmons described a light cake baked in small cups in her 1796 book American Cookery.
Eliza Leslie printed a recipe called cup cake in 1828; the name most likely comes from measuring by the cup.
The 1-2-3-4 cake is named after its cups of butter, sugar and flour and the four eggs that go with them.

fun_chocolate_covered_anything_day.intro: Strawberries, pretzels, crisps, coffee beans: if it holds still, it can be dipped. A day that treats chocolate as a coating rather than a food in its own right.
funFacts: Tempering gives chocolate shine and snap. Dark chocolate is often worked at 31–32 °C; milk and white chocolate need lower temperatures.
Enrobing machines replaced hand-dipping around 1900 and still pour a curtain of chocolate over passing sweets.
Japan has sold chocolate-coated potato crisps for decades, pairing salt with sugar long before it was fashionable.

fun_wright_brothers_day.intro: On 17 December 1903, the Wright brothers achieved the first powered, controlled and sustained airplane flights. Their first flight lasted twelve seconds: a short trip with an enormous place in aviation history.
funFacts: The first flight at Kill Devil Hills lasted 12 seconds and covered about 36 metres, the wingspan of a short-haul jet today.
The fourth attempt on the same day stayed up for 59 seconds and covered 260 metres.
Wilbur and Orville financed their experiments with the bicycle shop they ran in Dayton, Ohio.

fun_i_love_honey_day.intro: A day for the jar at the back of the cupboard: honey, the only sweetener made by insects, stirred into tea, spread on bread or eaten straight off the spoon.
funFacts: For 500 grams of honey, bees visit around two million flowers and fly some 90,000 kilometres between them.
Honey keeps for a long time when properly stored in a tightly sealed container, but excess moisture can allow it to ferment.
A single worker bee produces about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire life.

fun_holly_day.intro: A pun with a plant attached. The day celebrates holly, the glossy evergreen with spiny leaves and bright red berries that turns up on every winter wreath.
funFacts: Holly is dioecious: only female plants carry berries, and only if a male plant grows somewhere nearby.
The berries are mildly poisonous to people but see blackbirds and thrushes through the winter.
Lower leaves are spiky while the higher ones are often smooth, an adaptation against grazing animals.

fun_cortado_day.intro: Espresso cut with an equal measure of warm milk: strong enough to taste, soft enough to drink slowly. A small glass with a large following.
funFacts: The name comes from the Spanish cortar, to cut, because the milk cuts the sharpness of the espresso.
In the United States it is often served in a Gibraltar, a small tumbler borrowed from a San Francisco café.
In the Basque Country the same drink is ordered as an ebaki, which means exactly the same thing.

fun_crossword_puzzle_day.intro: On 21 December 1913 a newspaper printed the first crossword, and a whole species of puzzle was born. Best marked with a pencil and one stubborn corner.
funFacts: Arthur Wynne's first word-cross appeared in the New York World in 1913 and was diamond-shaped rather than square.
The New York Times long dismissed crosswords as a waste of time and only began printing them in 1942.
In 1942 Britain's Daily Telegraph ran a crossword contest and quietly approached the fastest solvers for codebreaking.

fun_mathematics_day.intro: India marks the birthday of Srinivasa Ramanujan, the self-taught mathematician who filled notebooks with results nobody could explain. A day for numbers and for curiosity.
funFacts: Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 and had almost no formal training in mathematics.
He left behind some 3,900 results, and mathematicians were still proving them decades after his death.
The number 1729 became famous as the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways.

fun_festivus.intro: The holiday for the rest of us: no tree, no presents, just a bare aluminium pole and a chance to say out loud what annoyed you this year. Popularised on television, adopted in earnest.
funFacts: Festivus reached the world through the Seinfeld episode The Strike in 1997.
Writer Dan O'Keefe borrowed it from his own family; his father had celebrated a version of it since the 1960s.
The ritual has two parts: the Airing of Grievances at dinner and the Feats of Strength afterwards.

fun_eggnog_day.intro: Eggs, cream, sugar, spice and usually a splash of something stronger. Eggnog gets its day at the height of the season, when the punch bowl is already out.
funFacts: Eggnog descends from posset, a medieval English drink of hot milk curdled with ale or wine.
One explanation for nog is the noggin, a small carved wooden cup once used for serving drinks.
The recipe from George Washington's household at Mount Vernon called for rye whiskey, rum and sherry all at once.

fun_pumpkin_pie_day.intro: A slice of spiced pumpkin custard in a pastry shell, on a day when the oven is running anyway. Cinnamon, ginger and cloves do most of the work.
funFacts: Early European cooks hollowed out a pumpkin, filled it with spiced milk and baked the whole thing in the embers.
Amelia Simmons printed two pompkin pudding recipes in American Cookery in 1796.
Most tinned pumpkin sold in the United States is made from Dickinson squash rather than the orange carving type.

fun_candy_cane_day.intro: Red and white, hooked at the top and impossible to eat quickly. The candy cane gets its day right after Christmas, while the tree is still full of them.
funFacts: They began as plain straight white sugar sticks; the hook and the red stripes only turn up around 1900.
A popular story credits a Cologne choirmaster in 1670 with the bent shape, though no contemporary source confirms it.
Bending the canes was hand work until Gregory Keller built a machine for the job in the 1950s.

fun_cut_out_snowflakes_day.intro: Fold the paper, snip a few notches, unfold and be surprised. A craft day for the quiet week between the years, and cheap decoration for every window.
funFacts: Real snow crystals grow six-fold because water molecules lock into a hexagonal lattice as they freeze.
Farmer Wilson Bentley photographed more than 5,000 snow crystals from 1885 onwards and never found two alike.
Folding the paper into six before cutting is the trick that makes a paper snowflake look like the real thing.

fun_card_playing_day.intro: The days between Christmas and New Year were made for card games. Deal out a deck, argue about the rules and watch the afternoon disappear.
funFacts: Playing cards reached Europe in the late 14th century, most likely by way of Mamluk Egypt.
The French suits of hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades were cheap to stencil and pushed the older designs aside.
A shuffled deck of 52 cards has more possible orders than there are atoms making up the Earth.

fun_tick_tock_day.intro: Two days left in the year and a list of things still undone. Tick Tock Day is the friendly reminder to finish at least one of them before the clock runs out.
funFacts: Early mechanical clocks in medieval monasteries had no hands at all and simply rang a bell at the right hour.
The pendulum clock built by Christiaan Huygens in 1656 cut the daily error from about fifteen minutes to fifteen seconds.
A second is defined today by 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a caesium atom.

fun_bacon_day.intro: Crisp, salty and loud in the pan: bacon gets its own day just before New Year. Breakfast plate, burger topping or straight off the kitchen paper.
funFacts: The word bacon goes back to a Germanic root meaning back or ham and reached English through Old French.
British rashers are cut from the loin, while American streaky bacon comes from the fattier belly.
That smell in the pan is the Maillard reaction, the browning chemistry behind bread crusts and roasted coffee.

fun_champagne_day.intro: The last day of the year is the one day when almost everyone reaches for the same bottle. Champagne gets its own date, cork included.
funFacts: A bottle holds around five bar of pressure, more than twice what a car tyre carries.
Dom Pérignon, a Benedictine cellar master, spent his career trying to get rid of the bubbles rather than create them.
Physicist Gérard Liger-Belair calculated about a million bubbles rising through a single poured glass.

fun_polar_bear_swim_day.intro: Le premier jour de l'année, les plus courageux se jettent dans une mer ou un lac glacé. Quelques secondes de cris, beaucoup de rires — et une histoire à raconter toute l'année.
funFacts: Chaque 1er janvier, environ 60 000 personnes participent au Nieuwjaarsduik néerlandais, une tradition née en 1960.
Depuis 1998, les nageurs néerlandais sont faciles à repérer : le sponsor Unox distribue des bonnets orange.
En Écosse, le Loony Dook se tient à South Queensferry, où beaucoup plongent déguisés.

fun_science_fiction_day.intro: Une journée pour les vaisseaux spatiaux, les machines à voyager dans le temps et les mondes impossibles. La date est l'anniversaire qu'Isaac Asimov s'était choisi lui-même, un clin d'œil à l'un des auteurs les plus prolifiques du genre.
funFacts: Asimov n'a jamais connu sa date de naissance exacte et a simplement décrété que c'était le 2 janvier.
Le mot « robotique » a été forgé par Asimov dans une nouvelle parue en 1941.
« Frankenstein » de Mary Shelley, publié en 1818, passe souvent pour le premier roman de science-fiction.

fun_festival_of_sleep_day.intro: Après le marathon des fêtes et des visites de famille arrive la mission la plus agréable de l'année : dormir. Rideaux tirés, couette remontée, réveil éteint — la sieste est officiellement au programme.
funFacts: Nous passons environ un tiers de notre vie à dormir.
Un cycle de sommeil dure à peu près 90 minutes et se répète quatre à six fois par nuit.
Les chats domestiques dorment douze à seize heures par jour, réparties en de nombreuses petites siestes.

fun_spaghetti_day.intro: Longs, fins et parfaits à enrouler autour de la fourchette : la journée appartient à la forme de pâtes la plus célèbre du monde. Sauce au choix, deuxième assiette prévue.
funFacts: Le nom vient de l'italien « spago », qui signifie ficelle.
En 1957, l'émission Panorama de la BBC a berné son public avec un reportage sur la récolte suisse des spaghettis.
L'Italie mène le classement mondial des pâtes : environ 23 kilos par habitant et par an.

fun_bird_day.intro: L'hiver est la meilleure saison pour observer les oiseaux : branches nues, mangeoires bien remplies et beaucoup de visiteurs. Une journée pour lever les yeux et tendre l'oreille.
funFacts: Les colibris battent des ailes jusqu'à 80 fois par seconde, ce qui leur permet de faire du surplace.
Les sternes arctiques migrent entre l'Arctique et l'Antarctique : des dizaines de milliers de kilomètres par an.
Les oiseaux sont des dinosaures vivants : ils descendent directement de petits théropodes à plumes.

fun_shortbread_day.intro: Trois ingrédients, un très bon biscuit : le shortbread écossais, c'est du beurre, du sucre et de la farine. Sablé, doré et fait pour accompagner une théière.
funFacts: La recette classique suit la règle 1-2-3 : une part de sucre, deux parts de beurre, trois parts de farine.
Un shortbread rond découpé en parts s'appelle traditionnellement « petticoat tails ».
Son ancêtre est un pain biscuité médiéval, cuit deux fois, qui a reçu de plus en plus de beurre.

fun_tempura_day.intro: Une pâte légère comme une plume, de l'huile brûlante, un peu de patience : la tempura transforme crevettes, champignons et haricots verts en bouchées croustillantes et dorées.
funFacts: Des missionnaires portugais ont apporté au Japon l'idée de la friture en pâte au XVIe siècle.
Le nom vient sans doute du latin « tempora », les jours de jeûne où l'on mangeait du poisson.
Dans l'ancienne Edo, la tempura se mangeait dans la rue : vendue en brochettes aux échoppes, debout.

fun_bubble_bath_day.intro: Eau bien chaude, une montagne de mousse et rien à l'agenda : le bain moussant est la façon la plus douillette de traverser janvier. Livre et bougie strictement facultatifs.
funFacts: La pellicule d'une bulle de savon ne fait que quelques centaines de nanomètres, bien moins qu'un cheveu.
Les bulles sont rondes parce qu'une sphère enferme le plus grand volume avec la plus petite surface.
Mr. Bubble, lancé aux États-Unis en 1961, a fait du bain moussant un classique de l'enfance.

fun_balloon_ascension_day.intro: La journée rappelle le premier vol habité en ballon au-dessus de l'Amérique du Nord, en 1793 — et donne une bonne raison de lever les yeux dès qu'une tache colorée traverse le ciel.
funFacts: Le 9 janvier 1793, Jean-Pierre Blanchard s'est envolé depuis la cour d'une prison de Philadelphie.
George Washington a assisté au décollage et remis à Blanchard une lettre de sauf-conduit.
Une montgolfière monte simplement parce que l'air chauffé qu'elle contient est plus léger que l'air extérieur.

fun_houseplant_appreciation_day.intro: Le sapin est parti, les décorations sont rangées — et les plantes d'intérieur, elles, sont toujours là. L'heure de l'arrosage, d'un coup de chiffon sur les feuilles et d'un peu de reconnaissance.
funFacts: Les feuilles de monstera se percent de trous pour que la lumière et le vent atteignent celles du dessous.
L'Angleterre victorienne a connu la « ptéridomanie », une véritable fièvre de collection de fougères.
En 1989, la NASA a testé des plantes d'intérieur en chambres closes pour mesurer leur effet filtrant.

fun_milk_day.intro: Une journée pour la boisson la plus banale du frigo — et pour tout ce qu'on en tire : le beurre, le fromage, le yaourt et la mousse du cappuccino.
funFacts: La date rappelle les débuts de la livraison à domicile, quand le lait arrivait en bouteilles de verre scellées.
La plupart des adultes dans le monde digèrent mal le lactose : le tolérer à l'âge adulte est l'exception.
Il faut environ vingt litres de lait pour baratter un seul kilo de beurre.

fun_marzipan_day.intro: Amandes moulues et sucre, façonnés en petits cochons, en pommes de terre ou en simples pains : la pâte d'amande est la douceur qui survit longtemps aux fêtes.
funFacts: La pâte d'amande, c'est essentiellement des amandes et du sucre : la teneur en amandes fait la qualité.
Le massepain de Lübeck bénéficie d'une indication géographique protégée dans l'Union européenne.
Le persipan lui ressemble, mais se fait avec des amandons de noyaux d’abricot ou de pêche au lieu d'amandes.

fun_rubber_duck_day.intro: Jaune, couinant et insubmersible : le canard de bain est la plus petite vedette de la salle de bains. Aujourd'hui, il reçoit les applaudissements qu'il mérite depuis des décennies.
funFacts: En 1992, un conteneur de jouets de bain est tombé dans le Pacifique : les canards ont aidé à cartographier les courants.
La chanson d'Ernie « Rubber Duckie » est vraiment entrée dans les classements américains en 1970.
L'artiste Florentijn Hofman promène dans les ports du monde des canards hauts de plusieurs étages.

fun_dress_up_your_pet_day.intro: Écharpe, nœud papillon ou costume de dinosaure intégral : aujourd'hui, les animaux ont droit à une garde-robe. Règle numéro un — si l'animal n'aime pas ça, la séance photo s'arrête.
funFacts: L'autrice spécialiste des animaux de compagnie Colleen Paige a lancé cette journée en 2009.
Pour les races à poil ras comme les lévriers, un manteau d'hiver n'est pas un déguisement mais une vraie aide.
Aux États-Unis, les costumes d'Halloween pour animaux pèsent plusieurs centaines de millions de dollars.

fun_hat_day.intro: Bonnet, béret, chapeau melon ou bonnet à pompon : en plein hiver, le couvre-chef est à la fois pratique et une façon d’affirmer son style. Aujourd'hui, sortez le plus voyant que vous ayez.
funFacts: Le chapeau melon est né en 1849 chez les chapeliers londoniens Lock & Co., pensé pour les gardes-chasse.
L'expression « mad as a hatter » renvoie au mercure autrefois utilisé pour feutrer les chapeaux.
Le panama est tressé en Équateur et ne doit son nom qu'à son escale sur la route de l'exportation.

fun_nothing_day.intro: Une journée sans programme : rien à fêter, rien à commémorer, rien à organiser. Volontairement la case la plus vide du calendrier.
funFacts: Le chroniqueur Harold Pullman Coffin a proposé ce non-événement en 1972 ; on l'observe depuis 1973.
L'idée était de contrebalancer le flot toujours plus grand de journées spéciales dans le calendrier.
Les Néerlandais ont un mot pour l'oisiveté assumée : « niksen », ne rien faire volontairement.

fun_kid_inventors_day.intro: Certains des meilleurs objets du quotidien ont été imaginés par des enfants. La date est l'anniversaire de Benjamin Franklin, qui a construit sa première invention à douze ans.
funFacts: Benjamin Franklin, né le 17 janvier 1706, s'est taillé à douze ans des palmes en bois pour les mains.
La glace à l'eau vient de Frank Epperson, 11 ans, qui oublia dehors une boisson et son bâtonnet en 1905.
Chester Greenwood a inventé les cache-oreilles adolescent et les a fait breveter quelques années plus tard.

fun_winnie_the_pooh_day.intro: L'anniversaire de l'auteur A. A. Milne se fête comme la journée de sa créature la plus célèbre : un ours à la cervelle très modeste et à l'appétit de miel sans limite.
funFacts: A. A. Milne est né le 18 janvier 1882 ; son fils Christopher Robin a donné son nom au personnage.
Winnie doit son nom à Winnipeg, une vraie ourse noire qui vivait au zoo de Londres.
L'édition latine « Winnie ille Pu » est entrée en 1960 sur la liste des best-sellers du New York Times.

fun_popcorn_day.intro: Sucré ou salé, cinéma ou canapé : le pop-corn est le grignotage qui fait du bruit avant même d'être mangé. Une journée entière pour le maïs le plus bruyant de la cuisine.
funFacts: Un grain éclate vers 180 °C, quand l'eau qu'il contient se transforme en vapeur et fait sauter l'enveloppe.
Des restes de pop-corn vieux de plusieurs milliers d'années ont été trouvés dans des grottes du Nouveau-Mexique.
Charles Cretors a présenté la première machine à pop-corn ambulante en 1885.

fun_cheese_lovers_day.intro: Pâte molle ou pâte dure, doux ou corsé : le fromage est l'un des plus vieux aliments de l'humanité. La journée revient à ceux qui le mangent directement sur la planche — le pain est facultatif.
funFacts: Les plus anciennes traces de fabrication de fromage sont des passoires en argile vieilles de 7 500 ans, en Pologne.
Les trous de l'emmental sont l'œuvre de bactéries qui libèrent du gaz carbonique pendant l'affinage.
France, Islande, Finlande, Danemark et Allemagne arrivent en tête, avec environ 25 kilos de fromage par personne et par an.

fun_hugging_day.intro: L'une des idées les plus simples du calendrier : serrer dans ses bras les gens qu'on aime. En plein mois de janvier gris, cela vaut plus que n'importe quel cadeau.
funFacts: Kevin Zaborney a inventé cette journée en 1986 dans la petite ville de Caro, dans le Michigan.
Le câlin libère de l'ocytocine, l'hormone associée à la proximité et au calme.
Les études chronomètrent le câlin spontané moyen à environ trois secondes seulement.

fun_answer_your_cats_questions_day.intro: Les chats fixent, clignent des yeux et attendent visiblement quelque chose. Aujourd'hui, la règle est simple : répondre à voix haute, en phrases complètes, et prendre la conversation au sérieux.
funFacts: Les chats adultes miaulent surtout pour les humains et presque jamais entre eux.
Un ronronnement se situe entre 25 et 150 hertz environ — les chats ronronnent aussi quand ils vont mal.
Une trentaine de muscles animent chaque oreille : le chat la pivote de près de 180 degrés.

fun_handwriting_day.intro: Le clavier va plus vite, mais rien ne remplace un mot écrit à la main. Aujourd'hui, place au stylo, au papier et au plaisir d'une signature bien déliée.
funFacts: La date est l'anniversaire de John Hancock, dont la signature ample sur la déclaration d'indépendance fit date.
En anglais américain, « John Hancock » désigne encore familièrement une signature.
Aucune écriture ne ressemble à une autre : les experts comparent pression, inclinaison et rythme.

fun_belly_laugh_day.intro: Une journée consacrée au rire qui secoue tout le corps. Le mode d'emploi est agréablement simple : lever les bras et éclater de rire.
funFacts: La tradition veut qu'on rie à 13 h 24, heure locale, bras levés, où que l'on se trouve.
Le rire est contagieux : en groupe, on rit bien plus souvent que seul.
Chatouillés, les rats couinent dans les ultrasons — les chercheurs y voient une forme de rire.

fun_burns_night.intro: L'Écosse célèbre son poète national Robert Burns avec un dîner, des cornemuses et des poèmes déclamés à voix haute. Le haggis n'est pas seulement servi : on lui adresse un discours en bonne et due forme.
funFacts: Robert Burns est né le 25 janvier 1759 ; ses amis ont organisé le premier Burns Supper en 1801.
Le haggis entre au son de la cornemuse et se voit accueilli par le poème « Address to a Haggis ».
« Auld Lang Syne », chanté partout dans le monde au Nouvel An, vient de Burns.

fun_peanut_brittle_day.intro: Du caramel, des cacahuètes, un craquement bien sonore : le croquant est la friandise la moins compliquée qui soit. Il faut une casserole, un peu d'audace et des mains froides ensuite.
funFacts: Les cacahuètes ne sont pas des noix mais des légumineuses, et elles mûrissent sous terre.
Une pincée de bicarbonate fait mousser le caramel brûlant : c'est ce qui rend le croquant léger et cassant.
Le croquant existe partout : chikki en Inde, croccante en Italie, pasteli au sésame en Grèce.

fun_kazoo_day.intro: Le kazoo ne demande ni cours, ni talent, ni accordage. On fredonne dedans et il en sort un son comiquement nasillard — l'instrument le plus démocratique du monde.
funFacts: On ne souffle pas dans un kazoo, on fredonne : une fine membrane transforme la voix en son nasillard.
L'Original American Kazoo Company, à Eden dans l'État de New York, presse des kazoos en métal depuis 1916.
Comme il n'y a rien à doigter, le kazoo passe pour l'un des instruments les plus faciles à apprendre.

fun_puzzle_day.intro: Puzzles, mots croisés, devinettes et casse-tête : une journée pour tout ce qui vous occupe joyeusement pendant une heure. Le moment parfait pour une longue soirée de janvier.
funFacts: Vers 1760, le marchand de cartes londonien John Spilsbury colla une carte sur du bois et la scia : le premier puzzle.
Les premiers mots croisés ont paru en 1913 dans le New York World, imaginés par Arthur Wynne.
Les plus grands puzzles du commerce comptent bien plus de 40 000 pièces.

fun_croissant_day.intro: Croustillant dehors, aérien dedans et une pluie de miettes sur la table : le croissant est le meilleur argument pour se lever tôt. Aujourd'hui, il vaut un petit-déjeuner complet.
funFacts: Le croissant descend du Kipferl autrichien ; le boulanger viennois August Zang l'apporta à Paris en 1839.
La pâte est pliée encore et encore pour que des dizaines de fines couches de beurre gonflent au four.
En France, la forme est un indice : droit, le croissant est au beurre ; courbé, il est traditionnellement à la margarine.

fun_backwards_day.intro: Pull à l'envers, dessert avant la soupe, prénoms lus depuis la fin : le dernier jour de janvier inverse l'ordre des choses. C'est un classique des écoles américaines.
funFacts: Léonard de Vinci écrivait ses carnets en écriture spéculaire, lisible seulement dans un miroir.
En 2015, Aaron Yoder a couru un mile à reculons en 5 min 54,25 s, établissant alors un record Guinness.
Les palindromes fonctionnent dans les deux sens : « ressasser » se lit pareil à l'endroit et à l'envers.

fun_robinson_crusoe_day.intro: Un clin d'œil au naufragé qui a tout déclenché : le 1er février 1709, le marin abandonné Alexander Selkirk était recueilli sur une île perdue du Pacifique. Une journée pour les romans d'aventure, les rêves d'île déserte et la débrouille.
funFacts: Alexander Selkirk a survécu plus de quatre ans seul sur une île du Pacifique avant que deux navires anglais ne le recueillent en 1709.
Le Chili a rebaptisé son île Robinson Crusoé en 1966 ; l'île voisine porte le nom d'Alejandro Selkirk.
Daniel Defoe publia son roman de 1719 sans y mettre son nom : le livre se donnait pour les mémoires de Crusoé.

fun_groundhog_day.intro: Chaque 2 février, un rongeur ensommeillé joue les météorologues : si la marmotte voit son ombre, la tradition annonce six semaines d'hiver de plus. Moitié folklore, moitié fête de village, entièrement réjouissant.
funFacts: La marmotte la plus célèbre est Punxsutawney Phil, en Pennsylvanie, où la cérémonie se tient depuis 1887.
Les marmottes hibernent vraiment : leur cœur passe d'environ 80 battements par minute à quelques-uns seulement.
Le film de 1993 avec Bill Murray a fait du « jour de la marmotte » une expression pour une journée qui se répète.

fun_carrot_cake_day.intro: Un gâteau qui fait passer des légumes pour un dessert — et qui s'en sort très bien. La journée célèbre ce classique moelleux et épicé, meilleur sous une épaisse couche de glaçage au fromage frais.
funFacts: Au Moyen Âge, on sucrait les entremets avec des carottes, car le sucre était rare et cher.
Le gâteau aux carottes s'est imposé au Royaume-Uni pendant le rationnement, quand le ministère vantait la carotte comme sucrant.
Les carottes étaient à l'origine violettes, blanches ou jaunes ; les variétés orange sont bien plus tardives.

fun_homemade_soup_day.intro: Une casserole, ce qui traîne dans le frigo et une heure de doux frémissement. La journée de la soupe maison réchauffe les jours froids de février et rappelle que les meilleures recettes se passent de recette.
funFacts: La soupe est l'un des plus vieux plats chauds : on a trouvé en Chine des marmites vieilles d'environ 20 000 ans.
Le mot « restaurant » vient de « restaurer » : au XVIIIe siècle, on vendait à Paris des bouillons fortifiants sous ce nom.
Une célèbre étude du Nebraska a montré que le bouillon de poule freine vraiment certaines cellules inflammatoires.

fun_chocolate_fondue_day.intro: Du chocolat tiède, de longues fourchettes et une table couverte de fruits : la fondue transforme le dessert en activité collective. Une façon très conviviale de passer une soirée de février.
funFacts: La fondue au chocolat est récente : un chef suisse l'a créée dans les années 1960 dans son restaurant new-yorkais.
Son ancêtre, la fondue au fromage, a été érigée en plat national suisse par la filière fromagère dans les années 1930.
L'usage veut que celui qui perd son morceau dans le caquelon doive une chanson ou la prochaine tournée.

fun_chopsticks_day.intro: Deux simples bâtonnets qui nourrissent une bonne partie du monde depuis des millénaires. Une journée pour le plus élégant des couverts — et pour s'entraîner à attraper un seul grain de riz.
funFacts: Les baguettes sont apparues en Chine il y a plus de 3 000 ans, d'abord comme ustensiles de cuisine, pas de table.
Les styles varient : courtes et pointues au Japon, longues et émoussées en Chine, souvent métalliques en Corée.
Planter ses baguettes à la verticale dans un bol de riz est tabou : cela évoque l'encens brûlé aux funérailles.

fun_send_a_card_to_a_friend_day.intro: Pas d'occasion, pas de raison, juste quelques lignes écrites à la main dans une enveloppe. Cette journée pousse gentiment à envoyer du vrai courrier plutôt qu'un message de plus, perdu dans une conversation.
funFacts: La première carte de Noël commerciale a été imprimée à Londres en 1843 pour Henry Cole, à environ 1 000 exemplaires.
Le Penny Post britannique de 1840 a rendu le courrier abordable et lancé la grande vogue victorienne des cartes.
Malgré les mails et les messageries, les foyers américains achètent encore des milliards de cartes chaque année.

fun_kite_flying_day.intro: Du vent, une ficelle et quelque chose de coloré qui danse dans le ciel. La journée du cerf-volant invite à sortir en plein hiver et à regarder en l'air un bon moment.
funFacts: On faisait voler des cerfs-volants en Chine il y a environ 2 500 ans, bien avant que le papier ne s'impose.
Avant l'avion, les services météo envoyaient leurs instruments en altitude accrochés à des cerfs-volants.
Alexander Graham Bell a bâti d'immenses cerfs-volants tétraédriques capables de soulever une personne.

fun_pizza_day.intro: De la pâte, de la tomate, du fromage — et des débats sans fin sur la bonne garniture. La journée de la pizza célèbre le plat napolitain qui a conquis presque tous les pays du monde.
funFacts: L'UNESCO a inscrit l'art du « pizzaiuolo » napolitain au patrimoine culturel immatériel en 2017.
Une vraie pizza napolitaine ne cuit que 60 à 90 secondes au feu de bois, à bien plus de 400 degrés.
Que la margherita ait été créée en 1889 pour la reine Marguerite de Savoie est une belle légende, non prouvée.

fun_umbrella_day.intro: Un petit toit portatif qu'on ne remarque que le jour où on l'oublie. La journée du parapluie honore l'un des objets du quotidien les plus sous-estimés — de préférence sous une bonne averse de février.
funFacts: Les plus anciens parapluies étaient des ombrelles ; les artisans chinois les ont imperméabilisés à la cire et à la laque.
Le mot anglais « umbrella » vient du latin « umbra », l'ombre : l'objet a été inventé contre le soleil, pas contre la pluie.
Le parapluie pliant de poche a été breveté en Allemagne en 1928 et vendu sous le nom de Knirps.

fun_make_a_friend_day.intro: Adresser la parole à quelqu'un de nouveau : au travail, dans la file d'attente, à la salle d'escalade. Cette journée rappelle discrètement qu'une amitié commence presque toujours par une première phrase un peu maladroite.
funFacts: L'anthropologue Robin Dunbar estimait qu'une personne peut entretenir environ 150 relations sociales stables.
Une étude de Jeffrey Hall (2018) suggère 50 heures ensemble pour devenir amis, et près de 200 pour être proches.
L'étude de Harvard sur le développement adulte a fait des bonnes relations le meilleur prédicteur d'une vie heureuse.

fun_darwin_day.intro: Charles Darwin est né le 12 février 1809, et son anniversaire est devenu une fête mondiale de la curiosité, de l'observation patiente et de la science en général. Pinsons, tortues géantes et très long voyage en mer inclus.
funFacts: Le voyage de Darwin à bord du HMS Beagle a duré près de cinq ans — et il a eu le mal de mer presque tout du long.
Avant de publier sur l'évolution, il a passé huit ans à étudier les balanes dans le moindre détail.
